assets.topic: Scrub the Foundations: What Self-Presentation Is and Why We All Do It
assets.visual_frame_description: A scrub-room montage: a parent's advice bubble saying 'Just be yourself' fades beside a mirror where a person adjusts their image; a ticker of disasters runs past, a funeral laugher, a swimsuit in the office, a job interview fail, while a cafeteria and a music store play out small courteous behaviors that keep images safe.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the raw material of self-presentation: define the process of controlling how one is perceived, expose why parents' advice to ignore others' opinions contradicts how we actually live, weigh the argument that self-presentation is healthy and adaptive rather than sleazy, and catalogue what happens to people who show no regard for others' impressions, from disparagement and ostracism to failed job interviews. Then track self-presentation in action, from the man recounting his college glory days to the cafeteria student who still does not grab food off others' plates, and see how impression management constrains almost everything we do.
key_concepts: Self-presentation, also called impression management, refers to the process of controlling how one is perceived by other people (Leary & Kowalski, 1990; Schneider, 1981; Schlenker, 1980).

Although Americans have a maxim that says we should rarely be concerned about others' opinions of us and should just be ourselves, virtually everyone thinks about other people's impressions of him or her from time to time, and some people worry a great deal about how others regard them.

The impressions people form of one another strongly affect how they respond to one another, so few social situations exist in which people can afford to disregard totally how others are perceiving and evaluating them.

Contrary to what our parents tried to teach us, self-presentation is not always a bad thing: rather than reflecting manipulativeness, vanity, or insecurity, paying an appropriate degree of attention to others' impressions is healthy and adaptive.
If people showed no regard for others' perceptions of them, they would fare quite poorly in life, because concern with others' impressions helps keep our behavior within socially appropriate limits.

People who were unconcerned with others' impressions would often behave inappropriately, resulting in negative reactions ranging from disparagement to ostracism, as when people laugh at funerals, wear swimwear to the office, or never bathe.

The tactless person who never impression-managed would have serious difficulties in job interviews and on first dates, and even if initially successful would have trouble keeping jobs, friends, and lovers.

A certain degree of attention to one's self-disclosures to other people is essential for the formation of close relationships, and people who do not convey an appropriate amount and type of information about themselves have difficulty developing and maintaining friendships and romantic relationships.

Although self-presentation is an essential component of social interaction, concerns with others' impressions can create difficulties, because people are sometimes too concerned about what others think of them or concerned in situations that are inappropriate.

People's self-presentational concerns can interfere with their performance on important tasks, cause them to feel anxious, and lead them to do things that are harmful to themselves or to other people, yet there is nothing inherently bad or sleazy about self-presentation.

Sometimes people act in certain ways primarily and explicitly to foster a certain impression, as when a man tells his date about his glory days as a college athlete, a student cleans up his apartment for his parents' visit, or a woman chooses clothes for a job interview.

Even when people's behavior is motivated by other goals, they typically pursue those goals in ways that do not jeopardize their image in others' eyes, so self-presentation provides a constraint within which most other behaviors occur.

assets.topic: Dialogue on Deception: Truth, Tactical Selection and the Unflattering Image
assets.visual_frame_description: A debate stage with two lecterns labeled TRUTH and DECEPTION, a spotlight sweeping over the professor's menu of true self-images, running shoes, a psychology textbook, a football; on a side screen the gruff boss's office, a street gang's alley, and a bored listener's frown flick past while a scale weighs positive impressions against intimidating ones.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue on how honest self-presentation really is: debate the liar who cons others, the exaggerator who claims wealth or intelligence, and the tactical selectors who pick only true self-images that serve their goals, then walk through the professor's own choices about mentioning running, psychology, or football depending on the listener. Press the case for believability and the anxiety of projecting false images, then turn the table to the unflattering side: the intimidating boss, the scary street gang member, the bore repelled by hostility, and people who want to be seen as incompetent, weak, or even mentally disturbed to get help or support.
key_concepts: You do not need a psychologist to tell you that people sometimes lie about themselves, and in extreme cases people may con others into thinking they are someone or something they are not.

More commonly, people may try to get others to form impressions that, although not completely false, are more positive than is warranted, such as impressions that they are wealthier or more intelligent than they really are.
Although some self-presentations are exaggerations and others are downright lies, most of the time the impressions people try to make on others are not deceptive.

Because we are all multifaceted individuals, in any given situation we could convey many different true impressions of ourselves, and rather than lying, people typically select the images they want others to form from their repertoire of true self-images.

The selection of images is often tactical in the sense that it is based on people's goals in the situation and on their assumptions about which impressions will best achieve those goals, but the impressions they try to create are more often accurate rather than deceptive.

Impression management usually involves accurate impressions colored by tactical changes in emphasis, tone, and omission, and the selection is sometimes completely self-serving but sometimes also for others' benefit, as when someone does not brag about running a marathon to a couch potato.

Schlenker and Weigold suggested that believability is a very important consideration when people construct their social identities, because if others do not regard the images people project as reasonably accurate constructions of reality, they will be dismissed as manipulative, deceptive, or deluded.

Most people find it anxiety producing to project and maintain public images that they know are not true, and because of these considerations, people project truly deceptive self-presentations only in rare instances.

In some cases, the impressions people try to convey are far from socially desirable, as when people want to be seen as threatening or intimidating because such impressions will help them achieve their interpersonal goals.

A boss may make sure his employees perceived him as gruff and intolerant to keep them in line, and a member of a street gang may dress and act in threatening ways so that people will be scared of him.

Most of us have tried to get rid of a bore by conveying an impression of hostility or disinterest, and people will even try to be seen as unlikable if doing so helps them achieve their goals (Jellison & Gentry, 1978).

The primary goal of self-presentation is not to be perceived positively per se, but to influence other people to respond in desired ways, and people sometimes think their interests will be best served if they can get others to perceive them as violent, incompetent, ill, or even mentally disturbed.

assets.topic: Audit the Founders: Goffman, Jones and the Ledger of the Field's History
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit desk on a 1959 timeline: Goffman's book is stamped FIRST ENTRY while theater curtains and props rise around it, and Cooley's quote is stamped SOLID FACTS OF SOCIETY; beside it Jones's laboratory bench holds a flattery experiment with a researcher recording subjects' ingratiating behavior while a list of his trained students is checked off one by one.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the origins of self-presentation research: check off how interest emerged independently in psychology and sociology, stamp Goffman's The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life (1959) as the starting point, and verify his claims that surface appearances are the solid facts of society, that people control others by managing the definition of the situation, and that interaction grinds to a halt when a public image is discredited. Then open Jones's ledger: the program of work on flattery, the insight that self-presentation is integral to interpersonal perception, and the shift from narrative essays to laboratory experiments, ending with the apprentices Jones trained who carried the field forward.
key_concepts: Interest in self-presentation emerged somewhat independently at about the same time in psychology and sociology, even though connections between the disciplines have traditionally been weak and researchers in each have typically relied little on each other's work.
The systematic study of self-presentation began with the work of sociologist Erving Goffman, whose major contribution was The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life, published in 1959.

Goffman's basic premise was that many of the most revealing insights about social behavior are to be found not in analyzing people's inner motives or personalities, but in studying the surface appearances people create for one another.

In the course of social life, people's responses to one another are heavily based on surface appearances, and Goffman's view was consistent with Cooley's (1902) claim that the imaginations which people have of one another are the solid facts of society.

For Goffman, people control how other people treat them by influencing others' definition of the situation, giving others the kind of impression that will lead them to act voluntarily in accordance with their objectives.

According to Goffman, self-presentation is not only functional for the individual but is essential for smooth interaction, because the public images people convey give other interactants some idea of how they expect to be treated and how they should expect to treat others.

Goffman seemed particularly interested in what happens when self-presentation goes awry: when the impressions people project are contradicted or discredited, the interaction is disrupted and often grinds to a halt until the person's public image is successfully restored.

Goffman has been associated with the dramaturgical approach because he made great use of metaphors of the theater, complete with acts, roles, props, audiences, and backstage areas, yet nowhere does he argue that life is nothing but a stage.

Goffman's work was more akin to social anthropology than sociology, his articles and books being essentially anthropological descriptions of everyday interactions in Western society, and he was an astute observer of human behavior.

At about the same time Goffman published his book, Edward Jones, a social psychologist, began a program of work on flattery, becoming involved with self-presentation because of his interest in how people figure out what other people are like.

Jones realized that our perceptions of other people are determined in part by their attempts to convey particular impressions of themselves, writing that we cannot understand how people perceive each other without understanding the dynamics of self-presentation.

Whereas Goffman reported what were essentially anthropological field observations in narrative essays, Jones and his students designed laboratory experiments to investigate specific factors that affect self-presentation, and Jones trained several social psychologists who went on to make contributions to the area in their own right.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Resistance, Spread and the Difficulty of Judging One's Impressions
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with columns labeled RESISTANCE, SPREAD and JUDGING; cards fly in, a colleague whispering 'as disreputable as parapsychology', a textbook index missing the terms, a balloon being popped, a hospital ward where patients appear more or less disturbed, a dissonance theory book being revised, and a conversation where a would-be intellectual comes across as pompous and vain.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a matrix of the field's growing pains: file the resistance cards, the colleague who compared self-presentation to parapsychology, the missing index entries in textbooks, the view of it as manipulative, the cognitive turn that demoted motives, and the theorists who punched holes in everyone else's balloons, alongside the pop psychology taint. Then file the spread cards: the early studies of status and social feedback, the hospitalized schizophrenics managing impressions, Tedeschi's dissonance reinterpretation, and the mid-1980s verdict that few interpersonal behaviors escape self-presentation. Finally, slot in the judging cards: calculated versus secondary impressions, the pompous egghead, the doubted honesty, and the overestimated consistency of others' perceptions.
key_concepts: When Jones first became interested in self-presentation in the early 1960s, some of his colleagues seemed to feel that he had entered a domain of investigation that was as unsettling and almost as disreputable as parapsychology.

One manifestation of the disinterest in self-presentation was that, until recently, it was difficult to find the terms self-presentation or impression management in the indexes of most textbooks on social psychology.

Part of the resistance may have come from the fact that many psychologists initially viewed self-presentation as inherently manipulative and deceptive, the ugly underbelly of interpersonal life, and thus regarded the topic as unsavory or unnecessarily narrow.

During the past 20 years, social psychology has been dominated by an interest in cognitive processes, and motivational processes have taken a back seat, which attracted less attention to the study of people's interpersonal motives.

During the 1970s, some researchers became frustrated because self-presentation theorists offered impression management as an alternative to accepted explanations of many interpersonal phenomena, and it seemed to some that the self-presentation perspective could explain almost anything.

Discussion of self-presentational strategies often sounded too much like the how-to-manipulate-others vein of pop psychology, so many viewed impression management as an inherently applied topic more appropriately studied by politicians, advertisers, and business executives than by psychologists.

Initially, research focused primarily on identifying factors that affect the kinds of impressions people try to convey, including the effects of status, interpersonal goals, expected interaction, other people's evaluations, and social feedback.

One of the first applications of self-presentational concepts to other areas examined how hospitalized schizophrenics manage their impressions to appear either more or less mentally disturbed depending on the immediate social context (Braginsky, Braginsky, & Ring, 1969).
During the 1970s, James Tedeschi and his students proposed that many behaviors that were originally explained as reactions to cognitive dissonance may actually reflect self-presentational strategies.

By the mid-1980s, it was difficult to find an interpersonal behavior in which self-presentation was not occasionally involved, and recent applications of self-presentational approaches to business and organizational settings have further demonstrated their usefulness.

Because a given behavior can usually be interpreted in more than one way, people run the risk of conveying images other than those they wanted to make, so we must distinguish between the calculated impression a person wanted others to form and the secondary impression that was unintended.

People are not always good judges of the impressions they are making: they seem to have some idea of the kinds of impressions they generally make on others but are less accurate at determining how they are perceived by specific other people (DePaulo, Kenny, Hoover, Webb, & Oliver, 1987), and research suggests they also overestimate how consistently other people perceive them.

assets.topic: Boss Level: The Person, the Situation and the Overarching Framework
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena that is a courtroom where the person-situation debate is on trial: on one bench a wedding party and a funeral crowd, on the other two identical rooms holding two very different people; a hologram of the book's structure lights up with Chapters 2 through 9 stacked in four pillars labeled TACTICS, MOTIVATION, IMAGE FACTORS and CONSEQUENCES, and a final trophy labeled PREREQUISITE: KNOWING HOW YOU ARE PERCEIVED.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the debate over what really drives self-presentation: stand your ground on the person-situation question, showing that most behavior is a function of both, that the situation demands solemnity at funerals while individual personality, background, and physiology make two people in the same room respond differently, and that people differ in how much they impression-manage at all. Then clear the roadmap of the book: the four bodies of research, the tactics of Chapter 2, the motivating factors of Chapter 3, the five sets of factors in Chapters 4 through 8, and the worried reactions of Chapter 9, finishing with the summary that outcomes in life depend on how we are perceived and that successful impression management requires knowing how one is coming across.
key_concepts: Although much has been written over the years about the person-situation debate over whether personal characteristics or the nature of the situation matter most, most psychologists today would agree that the question is a silly one because most behavior is a function of both the person and the situation.

The nature of the situation exerts a strong influence on behavior: we act differently at funerals than at weddings, sometimes respond differently to superiors than to subordinates, and react differently in crowded than in uncrowded environments.

Each person brings to the situation his or her unique personality, background, and physiological makeup, so that two people in precisely the same situation may not respond in exactly the same way, as some people are outgoing while others are introverted and some try harder to please.

The impressions people try to create on others are a function of both the situation and the individual, so the situation can exert considerable pressure on people to present themselves in particular ways, as when we must appear solemn at a funeral no matter how good we really feel.

People differ in the degree to which they are concerned about others' impressions of them and, thus, the degree to which they impression-manage at all, and they also differ in how they want other people to see them.
If we step back and take a broad view of the entire research literature, most studies of self-presentation deal with one of four topics.

Some research is designed simply to demonstrate that a particular behavior is affected by people's concerns with others' impressions, and virtually any behavior can be used for self-presentational purposes, which is why Chapter 2 looks at the wide array of tactics people use.

A second body of research has investigated factors that motivate self-presentational behaviors, since the degree to which people manage their impressions differs across situations and time, and Chapter 3 addresses why people manage their impressions from a number of perspectives, including evolution.

The third and largest body of self-presentational research has dealt with factors that affect the kinds of impressions people try to make on others, and Chapters 4 through 8 examine the primary sets of factors that affect the images people try to convey.

People's self-presentations are affected by the norms of the immediate situation and the roles they play in social life, the values of the targets they want to impress, their current social image in other people's eyes, the instrumental usefulness of the impression, and aspects of their private selves.

A fourth body of research has dealt with the emotional and behavioral consequences that occur when people begin to worry about the impressions others are forming of them, and Chapter 9 concludes with a look at how people respond when they become particularly worried about their impressions.

People's outcomes in life depend heavily on how they are perceived and evaluated by other people, so they often monitor and regulate the impressions others have of them, and although people often fall victim to self-presentational miscalculations, knowing how one is being perceived is generally a prerequisite for successful impression management.

assets.topic: Scrub the Verbal Tactics: Self-Descriptions, Attitude Statements and Public Attributions
assets.visual_frame_description: A scrubber playhead sweeps across a 1950s movie set where the starlet slaps the leading man and cries I'm not that kind of woman, then freezes on Nixon's television frame declaring I am not a crook; beside it a ledger card lists what he said versus what he left out, while a speech bubble over a classroom shows a student groaning and rolling his eyes at an offensive lecture topic and a podium slides between audiences of professional women and veterans.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the verbal tactics of impression management: sort attributive tactics that claim a person possesses certain characteristics from repudiative tactics like the movie starlet's slap that deny being a certain kind of woman, then weigh the self-description ledger, the risky explicit claim of Nixon's I am not a crook against the safe indirect football-player remark, Goffman's over-communication of some facts and under-communication of others, and the questionnaire finding that people tactically leave items blank. Then audit attitude statements, the students' groans and eye rolls in the sexuality class, the intuitive politician who tailors attitudes to each audience, and the attributional tactics of the coach who blames himself, the group members who claim credit for success, and Janet Reno's magnanimous acceptance of blame after Waco.
key_concepts: Self-presentational tactics that attempt to convey that a person possesses particular characteristics or is a particular kind of person are called attributive tactics, whereas tactics that deny the person possesses particular characteristics are called repudiative tactics.

When the movie starlet of the 1950s stops the leading man's romantic advances with a slap and says I'm not that kind of woman, she is using a repudiative tactic that tells him the kind of woman she is not without saying much about the kind of woman she is.

Nearly any aspect of behavior can be controlled for self-presentational purposes, including one's clothing, the recounting of a personal experience, a well-timed laugh, or even one's choice of food at a restaurant.

The most straightforward way for people to convey information about themselves involves verbal self-descriptions of their personalities, likes and dislikes, previous experiences, accomplishments, families, occupations, emotional reactions, and fears.

In a given interaction a person has a nearly infinite variety of absolutely true facts he could reveal about himself, and what he chooses to say is heavily influenced by the kind of impression he would like the other person to have of him.

As a self-presentational tactic, explicit claims about oneself are risky, because people rarely reveal information about themselves so directly and listeners may be alerted to the possibility that the claim is tactical, if not deceptive, as when Richard Nixon announced I am not a crook.

People's self-descriptions are often indirect or tacit, as when a man discussing sports with a new colleague simply notes that football sure has changed since he played the game, allowing the colleague to be enticed into asking for more information.

As Goffman put it, self-presentation involves the over-communication of some facts and the under-communication of others, and people use these exclusionary self-presentation tactics when they think accurate self-descriptions will make an undesired impression.

When subjects in self-presentation research are told they may leave certain questionnaire items blank or choose which self-ratings they will show to another person, they tactically exclude information from their self-descriptions that would create an undesired impression.

The attitudes we express influence the impressions other people have of us, so a person may tactically express, misrepresent, or hide her attitudes to lead others to form certain impressions, as when she voices support for capital punishment and you infer far more about her.

Politicians talk about different attitude domains to different audiences and avoid attitudes a particular audience may find objectionable, and Tetlock reminds us that, in many ways, we are all intuitive politicians.

An attribution is a causal inference or explanation a person makes about the cause of a particular event, and when people make attributional statements to others their attributions clearly affect the kinds of impressions others form of them, as with a coach who blames himself for a disappointing loss versus one who blames the members of the team.

assets.topic: Dialogue on Strategic Memory: Remembering, Forgetting and the MUM Effect
assets.visual_frame_description: A stage with two podiums: on the left a comedian holds up a placard reading I forgot, on the right a student raises a hand in class beside a bubble showing a memory ledger with I.O.U. $10 crossed out; a scale tips a frown-faced messenger carrying a dark envelope against a beaming messenger with a gift box, while a calendar flip shows yesterday's attitude being erased.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue on memory as a self-presentational instrument: open with Steve Martin's two-word escape hatch I forgot, then debate strategic remembering, the students who speak up to display knowledge, and Gentry and Herrman's memory contrivances in which people distort, reconstruct, or fabricate memory performances, including pretending to recall a stranger, pretending to forget the unpaid rent, and the magnanimous Oh, I had forgotten you owed me $10. Then cross-examine the forgetting of initial attitudes after counterattitudinal behavior and whether the motive is consistency or the wish not to look inconsistent, hypocritical, or unstable, and close with the MUM effect: why messengers fear bad news and why recipients like the bearers of good tidings even when they neither caused nor endorsed the message.
key_concepts: Comedian Steve Martin once recommended in one of his routines that people can get out of many difficult situations in life with two simple words: I forgot.

People can manage their impressions through strategic remembering and forgetting, as when students speak up in class as much to demonstrate their knowledge or insight to the teacher or other students as to educate those who are present.
A memory contrivance is an act in which people distort, reconstruct, or fabricate memory performances as they interact with others in order to achieve social goals.
People may pretend to recall meeting someone they don't really remember or act like their failure to meet some obligation was due to factors other than that they simply forgot it.
It is sometimes better to seem to have forgotten to do something, such as not paying the rent, than to admit you remembered but purposefully didn't do it.
Appearing to forget something can sometimes make a person look magnanimous, as when a person says Oh, I had forgotten you owed me $10.
Research has shown that people who behave in a manner that is inconsistent with their existing attitudes sometimes forget what their initial attitudes really were.

Recent data suggest that forgetting one's initial attitude after acting inconsistently with it is sometimes due to self-presentational motives, because people want other people to think they always believed in what they did so as not to look inconsistent, hypocritical, or unstable.
People seem to be more concerned about appearing inconsistent to others than they are with feeling inconsistent.

Just as people associate and disassociate themselves from other people, they associate and disassociate themselves from events, trying to be associated with good news but disassociating themselves from bad news, a phenomenon known as the MUM effect.
People prefer not to communicate bad news to others not so much because they feel uncomfortable about it but because they are worried that the recipient of the bad news will evaluate them negatively.

People like those who communicate favorable information better than those who tell them unfavorable things, even when the recipient of the information understands that the conveyer neither caused nor endorsed the unfavorable information.

assets.topic: Audit the Silent Channel: Nonverbal Behavior, Emotional Expression, Appearance and Gesture
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit gallery of mirrors: a smile-meter scans a woman smiling as she asks for a favor and a bowler beaming after a strike in front of a crowd while a lab stamp reads polite versus genuine; a catwalk of two mannequins, one in a three-piece business suit and one in greasy kneeless jeans with a dirty Grateful Dead T-shirt, and a power checklist with a straight-backed, steady-eyed figure beside a slouched, shifty-eyed one.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the nonverbal channels of self-presentation: tick off DePaulo's inventory of expressions, appearance, gaze, body position, and gestures, then hold Laux and Weber's emotion presentation up to the light, checking the smile ledger, the extra smiles when asking for help, courting a liking, and bowling a strike in public, the polite smile that can be told from genuine pleasure, and why people who impression-manage deny anger. Then walk the appearance gallery: the attractive are seen as more sociable, dominant, intelligent, socially skilled, and adjusted, the comb, makeup, and ironing board test, the three-piece suit versus the dirty Grateful Dead T-shirt, and the hire, promote, demote, and fire power of shoes and socks, and close on the power posture of the person who stands erect, gazes directly, and moves with force.
key_concepts: Through their nonverbal behaviors, such as expressions, appearance, gaze, body position, and gestures, people can express information regarding their personalities, moods, opinions, and physical and psychological states.
Laux and Weber introduced the term emotion presentation to refer to expressive reactions that are used to project images of oneself to others.

Research shows that people smile more when they ask another person for help or when they are trying to get another person to like them, and they are more likely to smile after bowling a strike if their faces are visible to other people.

Research shows that polite smiles can be distinguished from smiles of happiness or pleasure, suggesting that we sometimes smile not because we are happy but because we want to convey an impression of friendliness.

People tend to make better impressions on others when they express emotions that are appropriate for the situation than when they express inappropriate emotions, which is why award show losers appear as pleased as the winners announced in their place.

Because people who express positive emotions are perceived more favorably than those who express negative emotions, people may try to give others the impression that they feel better than they really do.

People who are particularly motivated to impression-manage are more likely to deny that they experience negative emotions, such as anger, than people who are less concerned with others' impressions of them.

People use their nonverbal expressions to convey information about the nature or quality of their relationships, and a couple may even use smiling, eye contact, and touching to convey to others that their relationship is stable when, in fact, it is not.

Compared to less attractive persons, attractive people are perceived as more sociable, dominant, intelligent, socially skilled, and adjusted, which is why people invest so much time, effort, money, and worry in trying to look good.

If our motivation to make impressions suddenly disappeared, we would be less likely to use combs, makeup, and ironing boards, even though we rarely consciously think of these acts as self-presentational.

People's impressions of others are heavily influenced by the clothes they wear, and people are sometimes hired, promoted, demoted, and fired based on nuances such as the kind of shoes or socks they wear.

People use gestures and bodily movements to convey impressions of themselves, and some people tactically control their posture, gaze, steadiness, and forcefulness to convey an impression of being a powerful individual.

assets.topic: Matrix of Association and Setting: BIRGing, CORFing, Conformity, and the Physical Environment
assets.visual_frame_description: A four-cell wall matrix: cell one shows fans in team jackets under a scoreboard with a widening victory margin, cell two shows a yard sign being taken down after an election defeat and a small locked closet door with a faded family crest, cell three shows a birthday-cake card labeled Rasputin above a glowing portrait, and cell four shows a diffused-light office where a visitor sits beside a desk while a wooden desk and a wall of world-city clocks loom; below, a seating chart marks a leader at the table head and a loner in the rear corner.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a matrix of the indirect tactics: drop the school-identifying apparel card into BASKING IN REFLECTED GLORY, noting the bigger the margin of victory the more team shirts appear, drop the hauled-down election sign and the hidden countess into CUTTING OFF REFLECTED FAILURE, file the Rasputin birthday subjects under BURNISHING and BOOSTING, and place balance theory in the center cell. Then run the conformity ledger: the restaurant tip, the door-in-the-face request, and the washed-out bridge, and finally stage the physical environment, sorting the professor's cluttered office, the BMW versus the old pick-up, and the theater's sets, props, and lighting, with the large wooden desk, the world-city clocks, the small appointment calendar, the visitor seated beside the desk, the pre-chosen headstone, and the head-of-the-table versus rear-corner seating chart.
key_concepts: Self-presentation by association is an indirect form of impression management in which people strategically manage information about the people and things with which they are connected rather than managing information about themselves directly.

By connecting themselves with those whom others admire, people can bask in reflected glory, whether by dropping names or telling about their connections to famous people, or by wearing team-identifying apparel.

University students are more likely to wear apparel that identifies their school after the football team has won a game than after the team has lost, and the larger the margin of victory, the more students are likely to wear school-identifying apparel.

People cut off reflected failure by disassociating themselves from people of disrepute, and people who display candidates' signs in their yards are more likely to take the sign down if the candidate they support loses the election than if their candidate wins.

People increase the apparent value of people, places, and institutions with which they are already connected (burnishing) and minimize the unfavorable features of things with which they are associated (boosting), bragging about relatives, neighborhoods, hometowns, churches, and colleges.

In Finch and Cialdini's experiment, subjects who were led to believe they shared a birthday with the crude and debauched Rasputin subsequently described him more favorably than subjects who did not think they shared his birthday.

As balance theory suggests, people tend to perceive things similarly that are associated with one another in order to maintain a sense of cognitive balance or harmony, which is why even trivial social associations can be effective self-presentation tactics.

Because people who do not conform to group norms are often rejected, people may try to convey that they share other group members' attitudes and values, although conformity can also be informational, as when we follow other cars detouring around a washed-out bridge.

Many diners regularly leave a tip not because they really want to but because they'll be perceived as stingy if they don't, and the pressure is so strong that many people feel compelled to leave a tip even if the service was quite poor.

The door-in-the-face effect works by first making a large request that is sure to be rejected, which increases the likelihood that a second, smaller request will be granted, in part because the refuser does not want to be perceived as an unhelpful, inconsiderate person.

Three aspects of the physical environment used for self-presentational purposes are sets, such as the size of living and working spaces, style of furnishings, finishings, and color scheme; props, such as magazines, diplomas, and trinkets; and lighting.

People manage their impressions by where they sit, and people form different impressions of a student who sits in the front center of the classroom than one in a rear corner, while side-by-side seating connotes more friendliness than sitting across from another person.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Hidden Tactics in Helping, Aggression, Sport, Eating, Risk-Taking and Teamwork
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena built as five spotlighted stages: on the first a donation box under a bright spotlight multiplies coins sevenfold, on the second a gang circles a perceived insult while the most dangerous member is crowned with admiration, on the third a man at a gym door hesitates before aerobics while a dessert plate is pushed away, on the fourth two cars speed toward each other in a game of chicken as a risky stock chart spikes, and on the fifth a smiling couple walks a red carpet as a doctor and a letter-writer nod in the wings, each upholding the team's image.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the subtle tactics hiding inside ordinary behavior: take the helping gauntlet, the seven-fold donation boost under public eyes, the image-repair help after a bad impression, and the bystander who fears looking silly by rushing in when no help is needed, then the aggression arena, the threatening image that makes others do one's bidding, the gang honor insult that precipitates violence, and the dangerous gang member who is most admired. Then run the lifestyle course: the tennis-against-bowling stereotypes that steer sport choices, the man who avoids aerobics and the woman who avoids weights, the public exerciser who fears being seen overweight, the passed-up dessert, the game of chicken and the risky investment, the seat belt refuser who won't appear overly cautious, and finally the teamwork finale, the letters of recommendation, the physician's code of silence, the partner praised because her traits reflect on him, and the couple that puts on a positive face in public.
key_concepts: Although we might like to believe that people help one another because they are truly concerned about one another's well-being, many acts of helpfulness are actually motivated by the helper's own self-interest, and being helpful makes us feel better and avoids the guilt we would experience if we didn't help.
Satow showed that people donated seven times more money when others would be aware of how much they donated than when their donations were private.
People are also more likely to help other people after they've made a bad impression because doing so helps to repair their tarnished images.

People are sometimes afraid that they'll look silly if they rush to help another person only to find that they had misinterpreted the situation and the person didn't need help after all, so they may refrain from helping unless they are absolutely sure help is needed.

Some people behave aggressively to establish an image of being threatening so that others will do their bidding, and some instances of seemingly senseless aggression may serve this self-presentational function.

Retaliatory aggression preserves one's image in the face of physical or verbal attacks by showing others that one is not to be trifled with, and one study of gang violence showed that the most common precipitating factor was a perceived insult to the honor of the gang or one of its members.

People hold stereotypes about people who enjoy different sports, so people's choices of sport activities are sometimes affected by self-presentational concerns, as when most men are unwilling to go to aerobics classes or take ballet because such activities are not consistent with the image they want others to have of them.

What and how we eat is greatly affected by social factors, as people pass up an extra dessert they really wanted so others won't think they're a pig, and studies show that eating can be affected by self-presentational motives.

Risk-taking behaviors are sometimes motivated by self-presentation: some people, particularly young men, drive fast to make an impression on their friends, and the old game of chicken, in which two drivers speed toward one another to see who swerves first, is essentially a self-presentational game.

Some people seem unwilling to take necessary precautions to protect their safety, such as wearing seat belts in cars, life vests in boats, and helmets on motorcycles, because they don't want to appear overly cautious to others.

People sometimes work together as impression-management teams, as when co-workers do not publicly criticize one another in front of clients or customers, and in medical settings a code of etiquette specifies that one physician should never say anything to a patient that would call into question the competence of another doctor.

Most couples, for example, try to put on a positive face in public no matter how strained and unhappy their relationship really is, and members of a department may work together to convey a particular impression of the department to administrators.

assets.topic: Scrub the Functions: Influence, Self-Construction and the Emotions We Trade in Impressions
assets.visual_frame_description: A scrubber playhead sweeps across a montage: two strangers shake hands while a thought bubble shows one judging the other's ability, then the scene cuts to a rejected job applicant counting his bills, a gruff intimidating boss scaring a subordinate into submission, a new professor adjusting his robes before a lecture hall, and finally a prehistoric clan gathering around a fire where the gregarious stay close while a lone figure drifts toward the shadows.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the personal functions of self-presentation: how the impressions people make are a primary determinant of their outcomes in life, why social interaction is mediated by the impressions interactants form of one another, and how making a good impression raises the quality of daily life while self-presentational failures spread from social to financial and material consequences. Then weigh self-presentation as social influence and power in the Jones and Pittman sense, walk the conditioning of self-esteem and emotions on the impressions we think we make, follow the new professor who enacts professor-like behaviors to construct and maintain a private identity, and close the books on emotion regulation through approval, the negative state relief model, self-disclosure, and the evolutionary roots of caring what others think.
key_concepts: The impressions that people make on others are a primary determinant of their outcomes in life, and when people respond to us they are really responding to their impressions of the kind of people we are—our abilities, personalities, attitudes, and intentions.

Making a good impression increases the quality of one's daily interactions because people are simply more pleasant, accepting, and affirming when they interact with someone of whom they hold a positive impression.

Self-presentational failures can spread beyond social outcomes to financial and material consequences, because people who make bad impressions don't have as many friends and may have more trouble landing the job they want or getting raises and promotions once they get the job.

Much self-presentation can be regarded as a mode of social influence, specifically as a way of affecting how other people respond to oneself, and Jones and Pittman suggested that self-presentation serves to maintain or augment one's power in relationships with other people.

One person has power over another to the extent that his or her actions can get the other person to behave in certain desired ways, and people can exercise power by presenting certain impressions of themselves, such as appearing nice, cooperative, and friendly or gruff, intolerant, and intimidating.

Self-presentational failures often lower one's self-esteem and cause negative emotional reactions, whereas self-presentational successes typically raise self-esteem and cause people to feel good, so over time people become conditioned to experience negative emotions when they think they've made undesired impressions and positive emotions when they think they've made desired ones.

Engaging in self-presentation helps to construct and maintain people's private identities, because before one can really see himself or herself as a certain kind of person, one must enact behaviors that are consistent with being that kind of person.

Because conveying images of oneself leads to corresponding changes in one's self-concept, people's self-presentations help them internalize new roles, as when a new college professor presents images consistent with being a professor to solidify his or her new identity.

Self-presentation is such a well-ingrained habit—learned from an early age because the impressions that parents, teachers, and peers have of us do have implications for our well-being—that we find it difficult to be unconcerned with what others think even when we know it doesn't matter.

Self-presentation can reduce negative emotions and promote positive emotions, because being approved of and accepted by others makes most people feel good, and the negative state relief model proposes that people behave in ways that will relieve negative emotions and facilitate positive ones.

Negative emotions motivate people to talk about themselves to others, and just as a fever both indicates the presence of an infection and helps to fight it, self-disclosure both indicates psychological distress and helps to reduce the person's inner distress.

Researchers have begun to consider the possibility that the tendency to be concerned with others' impressions may have evolved because it promoted survival and reproduction, since early prehumans and humans who stayed with the clan and were integrated into the social group were more likely to survive, reproduce, and pass on their genes.

assets.topic: Dialogue on Why We Care When It Doesn't Matter: Identity, Emotion, Evolution and the Common Good
assets.visual_frame_description: Two silhouettes debate on a stage as evidence cards float between them: a man retching beside a bar with two women staring, a beach walker sucking in his stomach, a mirror reflecting a person imagining himself through others' eyes, a fever chart labeled self-disclosure, a white blood cell counting up as Pennebaker speaks, and a hunter-gatherer clan sharing food around a fire while Goffman's cog-and-wheel diagram spins in the background.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue on the puzzle of impression management with no stakes: why a man agonized for days after vomiting in front of two strangers outside a bar, and why beach walkers suck in their stomachs passing people they'll never meet. Debate the three explanations—self-esteem and emotions affected by merely imagining what others think, self-presentation as a tool for constructing and maintaining private identities through signification, and self-presentation as an ingrained habit. Then argue the emotion-regulation case with the fever analogy for self-disclosure and Pennebaker's immune findings, and close with the evolutionary and societal side: the hunter-gatherer past, the gregarious ancestors whose descendants we are, rejection through undesirable impressions, and Goffman's claim that self-presentation greases the wheels of interaction.
key_concepts: People sometimes impression-manage even in situations in which there seems to be absolutely no reason to influence other people's behavior and no direct implications of making a particular impression, as when a friend of Leary's agonized for days after vomiting in front of two women coming out of a bar.

Because behaviors that make good or bad impressions are often associated with changes in self-esteem and emotional state, our self-esteem and emotions can be affected by simply imagining what others think of us, which is why it hurts to imagine strangers groaning, laughing, or wretching at our physique as we pass on the beach.

A second reason that people impression-manage even when they have no reason to influence others' behavior is that engaging in self-presentation helps to construct and maintain people's private identities, and if other people signify that they perceive the person as possessing the characteristics of a role—a process called signification—it helps him or her believe that he or she really possesses those traits.

Self-presentation is such a well-ingrained habit that we find it difficult to be unconcerned with what others think even when we know it doesn't matter, because from an early age we learn that the impressions parents, teachers, peers, and others have of us do have implications for our well-being.

Because negative emotions motivate people to talk about themselves to others, distressed people end up talking more about themselves, and when researchers asked students differing in trait anxiety to talk about anxiety-arousing versus happy topics, highly anxious students disclosed more private information when speaking about anxiety-ridden topics.

Stiles compared the relationship between self-disclosure and psychological distress to the relationship of fever to physical infection: just as fever can indicate the presence of an infection, high self-disclosure may indicate psychological distress, and just as a fever helps fight the infection, self-disclosure helps reduce the person's inner distress.
Pennebaker and his colleagues showed that simply expressing one's feelings improves affect, reduces stress, enhances physical health, and even increases the functioning of the person's immune system.

For the two million years before recorded history early humans lived as hunter-gatherers, and early prehumans and humans who sought out the company of others, stayed with the clan, and were integrated into the social group were more likely to survive, reproduce, and pass on their genes than those who tried to strike out on their own.

Because we are the descendants of the most gregarious people who ever lived, we may possess a motivational system that prompts us to establish supportive relationships with others and that causes distress when those relationships are damaged.

One of the primary reasons that people are rejected or excluded is that others have formed undesirable impressions of them, because being perceived as immoral, incompetent, or otherwise socially undesirable is likely to weaken one's connections to other people, whereas being judged as moral, competent, and socially desirable increases the chances of being accepted, integrated, and helped.

A sociobiological or evolutionary analysis of the personal benefits of self-presentation helps to explain why self-presentational motives are so pervasive: even when no tangible outcomes exist, we continue to monitor how others see us because nature and nurture have combined to create self-presentational habits and because we stand to experience negative emotions and lowered self-esteem if we don't.

Goffman suggested that social interaction could not effectively occur if people didn't construct public identities, so a certain amount of self-presentation is essential for meaningful interaction and, from a sociological perspective, self-presentation functions to grease the wheels of interaction.

assets.topic: Audit the Four Levels: From Impression Oblivion to Impression Focus, and the Traits That Tune the Gauge
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger shaped like a four-stage gauge: needle one marks OBLIVION with a movie screen, a fire and a riot, needle two marks PREATTENTIVE with a cocktail party and a name heard across the room, needle three marks AWARENESS with a person viewing himself in others' eyes, and needle four marks FOCUS with a stage fright victim whose mind goes blank while a mirror shows a paraplegic labeled by his status and a makeup counter crowded with mirror-gazers.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit how people monitor others' impressions across a four-level continuum: check off impression oblivion and its two causes, compelling external events and interfering internal states, then the subjective self-awareness of a spellbinding movie or a riot and the deindividuation of the drunk or enraged, tick off preattentive impression scanning with the cocktail party effect and the boss whose frown snaps a mindless conversation to attention, then impression awareness in Wegner and Giuliano's tacit-other/focal-self state and impression focus with its stage fright, blank minds, and ironic self-defeat. Close the ledger with the trait-based dials: public self-consciousness and its correlates, and the master status condition that dominates how a person is seen.
key_concepts: Although in reality impression monitoring is a continuum, for heuristic purposes Leary treats it as four levels: impression oblivion, preattentive impression scanning, impression awareness, and impression focus.

In impression oblivion, the person is unaware at any level of how he or she is being perceived by other people or even of the possibility that others are forming impressions, and is thus dramaturgically unaware.

Events can be so interesting, threatening, or stimulating that people devote all of their attention to the external world and literally have no attentional resources left to ponder what others might be thinking, and the person's psychological state in such situations, such as watching a spellbinding movie or finding oneself in the middle of a riot, is one of subjective self-awareness.

A person who is drunk or in a drug-induced haze may give little thought to others' impressions, and the same is true of a person experiencing an intense emotion such as rage or ecstasy, so in such powerful states people often say and do things they later regret partly because they didn't consider others' likely reactions.

People who have temporarily lost their ability to think about themselves, whether because of compelling external stimuli or because of internal impediments to self-reflection, are in a state of deindividuation, in which they have difficulty monitoring and regulating their own behavior and are less concerned with others' evaluations of them.

More commonly than true deindividuation, people monitor others' reactions at a preattentive or nonconscious level, and the cocktail party effect demonstrates that the brain can monitor the environment at a nonconscious level even while conscious processing is devoted to other tasks, so that a person intently engaged in conversation suddenly becomes attuned when his or her name is mentioned.

People scan the social environment nonconsciously for information about how others regard them, and if impression-relevant cues are detected—such as a frown or a lack of interest from one's boss—the person may shift conscious attention to them and begin to wonder consciously what the other person is thinking.

Viewing impression monitoring as preattentive helps to explain why people are seldom consciously aware of thinking about others' impressions yet can become so quickly attuned to particularly good or bad appraisals, and why many people deny that they worry about others' impressions of them yet use self-presentational tactics so readily.

When impression monitoring occurs at a conscious level, people are in a cognitive state that Wegner and Giuliano called tacit-other/focal-self awareness, in which they view themselves from the perspective of others, and this is probably the state people are in when most deliberate self-presentation occurs.

In impression focus, every thought is focused on others' impressions, and in many cases of stage fright and test anxiety, people's ruminations over their poor performance and what others will think interfere with task-oriented thoughts, resulting in impaired performance, so that when people report their minds went blank they were actually thinking quite actively about how poorly they were doing.

People who are high in public self-consciousness—measured by the Public Self-Consciousness Subscale of the Self-Consciousness Scale—tend to think more about their physical appearances, reputations, and others' impressions of them, and compared with lows they are more attuned to others' evaluations, more accurate in assessing the impressions others have of them, more likely to conform in group situations, and more anxious in social encounters.

A master status condition is a personal characteristic that is culturally defined as central to the understanding of a person's character, such as being obese, deformed, or paralyzed or being academically gifted, exceptionally attractive, or very wealthy, and it tends to dominate others' impressions of the person, so a paraplegic can never be regarded just as a student but as the paralyzed student; Frable et al. found that people who possess such a condition are more mindful during interactions, thinking more about what the other person was thinking.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Goal-Relevance, Value of Desired Goals and the Desired-Current Image Gap
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with three columns labeled GOAL-RELEVANCE, VALUE OF DESIRED GOALS and DESIRED-CURRENT DISCREPANCY: cards fly into place, a bathroom mirror with a man combing his hair before a job interview, a teacher with a grade book towering over a student, a supervisor pointing at a worker about to sing, a job interview with fifteen applicants crammed at a table, an attractive stranger drawing stares, an embarrassed man whose friends look away, and a figure standing on winners' shoulders to bask in reflected glory while the equation rewards minus punishments glows at the bottom.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build the three-cell matrix of impression motivation: drop each evidence card into GOAL-RELEVANCE (publicity of behavior, private grooming and rehearsal for public performances, dependency on bosses and teachers versus friends, the supervisor who assigns the onerous Star-Spangled Banner task, and anticipated future interaction), into VALUE OF DESIRED GOALS (resource scarcity and the Pandey and Rastagi job competition study, the desirable target whose reactions matter more, and the approval value of the failure-embarrassed and the fear-of-negative-evaluation high), and into DISCREPANCY (failure and embarrassment motivating image repair, and the tactics of stressing other positive attributes, self-serving attributions, favors, and basking in reflected glory). Then place the summary card: people impression-manage to maximize rewards and minimize punishments.
key_concepts: At the most general level, the motive to impression manage springs from the same motivational source as all behavior—people impression manage to maximize rewards and minimize punishments—and three factors are particularly likely to motivate people: the goal-relevance of impressions, the value of desired goals, and discrepancies between one's desired and current image.

People are motivated to impression-manage to the extent that they think that conveying certain impressions will increase their chances of obtaining outcomes they desire, so in situations in which the impressions people make have few, if any, implications for their outcomes, the motivation to impression-manage will be low, if not zero.

Perhaps the most important determinant of goal-relevance is the publicity of one's behavior, the degree to which others might observe it firsthand or learn about it from secondhand sources: the more public one's behavior, the more relevant it is to the person's public image, and the more motivated the person will be to impression-manage.

Even behaviors that a person performs while entirely alone can be affected by self-presentational motives, because people may prepare privately for self-presentations they will later execute publicly, as when we shower, comb our hair, and dress in private partly because of the public impressions we will make later, or privately rehearse what they will say to someone else to make the right impression.

Dependency refers to the degree to which a person's outcomes are contingent on the behavior of another person, and when a person is dependent on others for valued outcomes, the impressions he or she makes are more important, so people are more likely to try to control how they are perceived by their bosses and teachers than by their friends, and subordinates ingratiate themselves with their superiors more than superiors ingratiate themselves with their subordinates.

In an experiment Leary conducted with Robin Kowalski, subjects playing the role of a company worker described themselves to a supervisor before task assignments, and their self-presentations were affected only when the supervisor had the power to assign them to the onerous or the nonthreatening task—that is, when subjects' dependency on the supervisor was high.

Other things being equal, people's impressions are more relevant to their attainment of valued goals the more they expect to interact with another person in the future, because when we expect to interact with a person repeatedly we realize the impressions we make may have implications for how we get along with that person for a long time to come.

Impression motivation may begin to decrease after people get to know one another well and interact again and again, and research showed that university students were less motivated to impression-manage in interactions with their same-sex best friends than with people of their sex they knew less well.

Just as the value of something typically increases as it becomes more scarce in economic systems, impression motivation is higher when resources are scarce, and a study by Pandey and Rastagi showed that people were more likely to ingratiate a job interviewer as competition for the job became more fierce.

People are more likely to manage their impressions when interacting with those who are physically attractive or otherwise socially desirable, because we value the reactions of people with desirable characteristics more highly and because attractive, powerful, competent, and high status people are often in positions to mediate important outcomes that we desire.

Because people who have recently suffered a blow to either their self-esteem or their esteem in others' eyes value approval more highly, failure, rejection, and embarrassment increase people's desire for social approval and thus their motive to impression manage, and people who score high in fear of negative evaluation or need for approval are generally more motivated to control how others see them.

The third factor that motivates self-presentation is the degree of discrepancy between the image one would like others to have of oneself and the image that others appear to hold, so people who have made undesired impressions are particularly motivated to impression-manage, using tactics such as stressing other positive attributes, making self-serving attributions for the events that damaged their images, doing favors for others, and associating with successful people to bask in reflected glory.

assets.topic: Boss Level: The Self-Monitor's Toolkit and the Motive That Works in the Dark
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena built like a costume closet: a wardrobe of hats swings open as a high self-monitor tries on personas while asking the mirror who this situation wants me to be; on one wall a To Tell the Truth monitor screens freeze as he points out the liar, on another a boundary spanner bridges a management-versus-labor chasm, and in the corner a low self-monitor stands frozen, insisting he can only argue for ideas he already believes, while a comb-in-hand figure absentmindedly grooms in front of a mirror.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the question of how much of self-presentation runs without conscious control: hold up the mindless habits like combing hair, catch the experiment in which subjects mirrored their partner's self-enhancement while insisting they would have presented themselves the same way anyway, and then master the self-monitoring gauntlet—Snyder's high self-monitor who asks who this situation wants me to be, the cue-sensitive reader of social situations who can spot the liar on To Tell the Truth, the disclosure matcher with a wardrobe full of styles, the boundary spanner and the emergent leader, and the low self-monitor who can only argue for ideas he already believes. Finish with the controversy over the Self-Monitoring Scale and its 18-item shortened version.
key_concepts: Some self-presentational behaviors are performed so regularly that they become mindless habits, so although the behavior may have begun because the person consciously wanted to create a certain impression, the person now performs the behavior without consciously thinking about its self-presentational roots, as when people comb their hair without consciously thinking that they'd better comb it so they'll look okay.

People sometimes engage in self-presentational behaviors nonconsciously because they are not consciously aware of the stimuli that are causing their behaviors: in one experiment, subjects who interacted with self-enhancing conversation partners presented themselves more positively than subjects who interacted with modest partners, yet the subjects seemed completely unaware that their own self-presentations had been influenced by those of their partners.

According to Mark Snyder, who first identified the construct and developed the Self-Monitoring Scale, a high self-monitor is a person who, out of a concern for social appropriateness, is particularly sensitive to the expression and self-presentation of others in social situations and uses these cues as guidelines for monitoring and controlling his or her own self-presentations.
As high self-monitors enter social situations, they seem to ask themselves who this situation wants them to be and how they can be that person.

Low self-monitors are not as sensitive to social cues regarding appropriate behavior and self-presentation, are not as capable of controlling the impressions others form of them, and attempt to manage their impressions less often than high self-monitors.

High self-monitors are more likely than lows to say that statements such as In different situations and with different people, I often act like very different persons and I may deceive people by being friendly when I really dislike them are true of them, whereas low self-monitors tend to endorse statements such as I can only argue for ideas which I already believe and I have trouble changing my behavior to suit different people and different situations.

Successful impression management requires that people successfully read the social situation for cues about how to respond, then adjust their behavior accordingly, and high self-monitors are better on both of these dimensions than lows.

High self-monitors are more likely to seek information about other people, pay more attention to information they learn about those they meet, are better at reading other people's emotions from their expressions, and are better than lows at detecting when other people are being manipulative and ingratiating, as when highs were more accurate than lows at identifying truthful from lying contestants on videotapes of the television show To Tell the Truth.

High self-monitors are more likely to use tactical self-presentation than lows, such as matching their level of self-disclosures to the self-disclosures of the people with whom they interact, and high self-monitoring men have more different styles of clothing in their wardrobes than low self-monitors, presumably using clothing to make different impressions depending on the social context.

Other people rate high self-monitors as more skillful than lows in controlling their social behavior and emotional expressions, and high self-monitors tend to be more successful in situations that require them to tailor their behaviors to specific features of the social context, such as boundary spanning positions in business organizations that require employees to interact with highly disparate groups like management and labor in contract disputes.
High self-monitors also tend to emerge as leaders in groups and organizations more often than lows, possibly because they are more flexible across different situations.

Although the Self-Monitoring Scale has generated a great deal of controversy because several studies showed the scale taps at least three distinct attributes that do not perfectly match Snyder's original conceptualization, Snyder and Gangestad offered a shortened 18-item version of the original 25-item scale, and most research supports Snyder's hypotheses regarding the relationship of self-monitoring to self-presentation.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Social Context: Norms and Roles

assets.topic: Scrub the Unwritten Rules: Norms, Roles, and the Birth of Self-Presentational Norms
assets.visual_frame_description: A crowded city bus where a man hesitates over an elderly woman's seat while a thought bubble shows an 'inconsiderate louse' label, then a ledger book labeled unwritten rules opens beside a funeral service with a smiling attendee marked deviant, a street-corner man declaring he is Jesus stamped outside a limit line, and five file cards labeled decorum, modesty, matching, consistency, and civil attention.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the unwritten rules of social life: how norms and roles have no physical existence yet govern much of our behavior, why Milgram's subjects found it agonizing to ask an elderly woman for her seat on a bus, and the chapter principle that people project images consistent with the norms of a setting and the roles they occupy. Then weigh the mechanics of self-presentational norms: a norm as an implicit, unwritten rule for action, the prescriptive norm of solemnity at funerals, the restrictive limits on what a man on a street corner may claim to be, the general norms whose violation brands a person unsocialized or rude, and the list of the five common norms that anchors the chapter.
key_concepts: Norms and roles have no physical existence: unlike laws, they are not written down in books or posted on signs, and typically no one explicitly forces us to follow their dictates, yet much of our behavior is a direct consequence of the fact that we behave in line with them.

In Stanley Milgram's studies, subjects asked to perform unusual actions such as requesting an elderly woman's seat on a crowded bus had great difficulty doing so, and those who managed the behaviors experienced intense feelings of social discomfort afterward.

After taking the elderly woman's seat, a person feels distressed not only because a social norm was violated but because the violation has self-presentational implications: the person simply looked like an inconsiderate louse.

The chapter principle states that, unless explicitly motivated to do otherwise, people try to project images of themselves that are consistent with the norms in a particular social setting and with the roles they occupy.

A norm is a rule or standard for action that is usually implicit and unwritten, as opposed to regulations and laws, which are more explicit, and norms specify not only how people should act but also the nature of the public images they should and should not convey in particular situations.

Norms that are relevant to the impressions people should convey of themselves are called self-presentational norms, and when such norms and roles are in effect people often tailor their self-presentations to comply with them.

Prescriptive self-presentational norms dictate particular impressions that should be conveyed, as at a funeral where norms prescribe that attendees maintain expressions of solemnity regardless of how they actually felt about the deceased.
A funeral-goer who smiled broadly throughout the service would be viewed as quite deviant even if everyone knew that he or she had just won the state lottery or was the deceased's worst enemy.

Restrictive self-presentational norms constrain or limit the possible images people may convey in a setting without indicating the precise impression to foster, so a man who stands on a city street corner and claims to be Jesus is not staying within the normative limits on who he may claim to be.

Some self-presentational norms apply to a broad range of social settings, and failure to maintain these general, omnibus impressions usually leads others to conclude that the person is unsocialized, rude, disturbed, or purposefully trying to appear deviant.
The five most common general self-presentational norms discussed in the chapter are decorum, modesty, matching, consistency, and civil attention.

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Four Norms: Decorum, Modesty, Matching, and the Consistency Battle
assets.visual_frame_description: A courtroom of norms where decorum refuses to pick its nose and a prisoner walks to execution with dignity, a scale tipping between typed on the computer all day and the self-presentation book I'm writing, a reciprocity meter forcing a stranger to reveal something personal immediately, and a debate podium where Festinger's dissonance triangle faces Tedeschi's consistency mask with a bogus pipeline machine humming in the corner.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue among the core self-presentational norms: put decorum on the stand for why we do not pick our noses, belch, or break down in public, even under the stress of an execution chamber; then let the modesty norm confess its dilemma, from braggarts and self-deprecation to describing the same act as typing all day versus writing a book, and the four cautions about when modesty actually works; then match the matching norms, the positivity norm of Gergen and Wishnov and the depth of disclosure norm that pressures strangers to reciprocate confidences immediately; finally stage the consistency debate, where Festinger's cognitive dissonance theory faces Tedeschi, Schlenker, and Bonoma's claim that attitude change after counterattitudinal behavior is really self-presentation, with the bogus pipeline and the desert island test as the deciding exhibits.
key_concepts: Decorum refers to behavior that conforms to established standards for proper behavior, and many of the most basic norms specify minimum criteria for socially acceptable behavior.

Many polite and socially appropriate things that people do and do not do in public are done and not done, not because they are harmful to anyone, but because of self-presentational norms, such as not picking one's nose, not belching loudly, and not interrupting others while they are talking.
Norm-violators are not only negatively evaluated but are sometimes outright rejected (Baumeister & Tice, 1990; Schachter, 1951).

Many self-presentational norms involving decorum are so strong that people try to abide by them even under extreme stress, and even prisoners who are being executed seem intent to die with grace even though no one could blame them for crying, shouting, cursing, or pleading.

The modesty norm puts impression managers in a dilemma: people usually want others to perceive them as positively as possible, yet self-presentational norms require that they not be too self-aggrandizing, and people who violate this norm are regarded as braggarts, boasters, show-offs, or megalomaniacs.

People who want to appear modest tend to describe their behavior at a relatively low level of meaning, such as saying I typed on the computer all day, whereas those who want to self-aggrandize describe the identical activity at a higher level, such as saying they worked on the self-presentation book they are writing (Vallacher, Wegner, & Frederick, 1987).

Four cautions about modesty are in order: it is more effective after the fact than before, slight modesty is more effective than extreme modesty, accurately stating that one did well while downplaying the importance of the performance is seen as boastful rather than modest, and downplaying accomplishments works only if others know the person actually did well.

The self-presentation positivity norm specifies that people should present themselves just about as positively as others in the interaction, as Gergen and Wishnov (1965) demonstrated when subjects who received egotistical self-ratings from another person subsequently described themselves more positively.

The depth of disclosure norm specifies that people should match the depth or intimacy of other people's self-disclosures: among strangers this effect occurs within single interactions, while among people who know each other well the norm operates over a longer time span.

The consistency norm dictates that people should behave consistently with their beliefs and attitudes and show a reasonable degree of consistency across different situations, and people who do not appear consistent are often viewed as weak, unreliable, hypocritical, deluded, or even mentally unstable.

In the classic study by Festinger and Carlsmith (1959), subjects who were paid a pittance for telling another person that a boring task was interesting changed their attitudes more than subjects who were paid handsomely.
