In the bogus pipeline studies of Gaes, Kalle, and Tedeschi (1978), subjects who believed a machine could measure their true attitudes admitted their real beliefs and showed no evidence of attitude change, whereas subjects not connected to the machine expressed attitudes more consistent with their essays.

assets.topic: Audit the Norms of Attention and Gender: From Civil Inattention to the Continental Airline Makeup Case
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger where a bored listener wears a fixed interested smile marked contrived, a restroom scene stamps civil inattention on two strangers ignoring each other, a party argument is stamped nothing unusual is happening, and a gender column lists dominant, ambitious, tough as approved for men but derogated for women, with a makeup jar and an airline badge crossed out beside a lighter plate of food.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the norms that police how much attention we may show and how each gender may appear: check off civil attention and Goffman's contrived involvement when a boring speaker drones on, then civil inattention with its oblique glances and hushed tones, the restroom greeting ritual, and the nothing unusual is happening norm with its three functions, from the arguing couple at the party to the ranting street person. Then open the gender ledger: breadwinner and child-care expectations, the double standard that makes dominant tough women look bad, sissies versus feminine little girls, why women are more self-revealing, eating lightly, the Continental Airlines ticket agent fired for refusing makeup in 1991, and why few men take aerobic dance while few women lift weights.
key_concepts: The norm of civil attention dictates that people appear to be at least minimally involved in social encounters, so when a conversation fails to capture spontaneous involvement, the person obliged to participate is likely to contrive an appearance of being really involved (Goffman, 1967).

The self-presentational norm of civil inattention specifies that people don't pay undue attention to things that aren't any of their business (Goffman, 1963), so we often glance at other people obliquely, listen to them while we engage in other behaviors, and talk about what they say or do in hushed tones.

The civil inattention norm is commonly in force when strangers meet in a public restroom: they glance at one another, perhaps nod or grunt a greeting, then pretend that one another is not there (Cahill et al., 1985).

A self-presentational norm closely related to civil inattention is that of nothing unusual is happening (Emerson, 1970): when a couple at a party becomes embroiled in an argument, or when we pass street people who are ranting loudly to themselves, observers are inclined to give the impression that they notice nothing out of the ordinary.

Conveying the impression that nothing unusual is happening serves several functions: it allows adherence to norms of inattention and politeness, it lets people avoid responding to situations that may be awkward or dangerous, and it helps people stall for time until they figure out how to respond.

In every society, norms specify that men and women should engage in a somewhat different range of behaviors, with men expected to be the primary breadwinners and women expected to take primary responsibility for the children in most societies around the world.

People often think that men should appear dominant, ambitious, assertive, and tough, but those same people may view dominant, ambitious, assertive, tough women negatively, whereas a sensitive and emotional woman may make a good impression while a sensitive and emotional man may not.

From an early age boys and girls are rewarded for creating different public images: little boys are encouraged to act independent and are teased for looking like sissies, while little girls are encouraged to be expressive and nurturant and to act feminine (Deaux & Major, 1987).

Adult men present themselves as more assertive, powerful, and competent than women, whereas women's self-presentations emphasize their interpersonal and communal attributes (Deaux, 1977; Forsyth, Schlenker, Leary, & McCown, 1985).

Because eating lightly is associated with appearing feminine in American society, women are more likely than men to eat less when they want to make socially desirable impressions, and one study showed university women were particularly likely to reduce how much they ate when eating with a man whom they thought perceived them as unfeminine (Pliner & Chaiken, 1990; Mori et al., 1987).

Self-presentational norms even require that men and women groom differently: most American women wear makeup when they go into public, but men who wear makeup are openly ridiculed, and in 1991 Continental Airlines fired a ticket agent because she refused to wear makeup and lipstick until she threatened to sue for sexual harassment (Goodman, 1991).

Because people who engage in activities associated with the other gender are often ridiculed, some people will not engage in them, which helps explain why so few men become involved in aerobic dance or ballet and why relatively few women box or lift weights (Leary, 1992).

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Context-Specific Norms, Culture, Roles, and Prototype Correspondence
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with four columns labeled CONTEXT NORMS, CULTURE, ROLES, and PROTOTYPE; cards fly into place, a wedding cake beside a funeral wreath, a group nodding in unison while a lone dissenter is ostracized, a globe split between moderating adverbs and a drummer, a minister's collar and a party host's nametag, and a presidential podium showing a surgical scar, a stuck voting machine, and a Miami model crashing a candidacy, while a sink faucet runs with a crowd icon and a solitary icon.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a four-cell matrix for the social context: drop each evidence card into its cell, the wedding-versus-funeral expressions and the cohesive group's pressure to appear to agree with public rather than anonymous opinions into CONTEXT-SPECIFIC NORMS; the conformity culture with its moderating adverbs and the self-direction culture marching to its own drummer into CULTURE; the definition of a role as a norm attached to a position, the permanent parent or minister versus the party host, and the clergy's required image of caring selflessness into ROLES; and the cognitive prototypes of Cantor and Mischel, the LBJ surgical scar and FDR's cursed voting machine as minor violations, and Gary Hart's doomed 1988 campaign as the fatal one into PROTOTYPE CORRESPONDENCE. Then place the restroom card showing hand-washing more likely when others are present.
key_concepts: The variety of context-specific self-presentational norms is virtually endless, as shown by the fact that the norms for a funeral differ from those of a wedding: wedding guests are expected to look happy, whereas mourners are not, even if the wedding guests are actually more unhappy than the mourners.

In highly cohesive groups, in which there is a great deal of we-feeling, norms discourage behaviors that threaten the group's solidarity, and people who rock the boat are ignored, devalued, or ostracized.

Group members feel pressure to appear to agree with other group members even when they privately disagree, and the fact that people are more likely to express opinions that go along with the group when they express their opinions publicly rather than anonymously shows that conformity is heightened by self-presentational motives (Deutsch & Gerard, 1955).

Confusion and misunderstanding can arise when people from one culture engage in self-presentations that do not conform to the norms of another culture, so a person may behave in a certain way to communicate a certain impression yet find that persons from another culture draw an entirely different impression from the one intended.

One way to examine self-presentational norms across cultures is to consider the personal characteristics that different cultures value, and cultures differ in the degree to which they value achievement, power, hedonism, respect for tradition, and conformity (Schwartz & Bilsky, 1987).

In a culture that values conformity, people will pretend to agree more than they really do, use a large number of moderating adverbs to qualify their statements such as slightly and perhaps, and avoid taking strong positions against the group.

In a culture that values self-direction, people will be freer to express their true opinions and emotions, more likely to experiment with their lifestyles, more willing to march to the beat of their own drummer, and may go out of their way not to give the impression of being overly provincial, conservative, or traditional.

A social role is a set of behaviors that is associated with a particular position within a social system, and you can think of roles as a special kind of norm, specifically a norm that is attached to a particular position or part (Turner, 1990).

Some roles, such as parent or minister, are relatively permanent and transcend situations and time, whereas in other cases people enact a role only for a specified period of time or for a particular occasion, as when a person enacts the role of host for the duration of the party, after which the role ceases to exist.

Many roles prescribe not only how people in a certain position are to behave but that people who occupy the position should appear to be a certain kind of person, so a minister, priest, or rabbi must be seen as caring, more selfless than the average person, highly moral, and even-tempered, while not being seen as overly hedonistic, carefree, or earthy.

Role-determined self-presentations are governed by a process of prototype correspondence: people hold cognitive prototypes regarding categories of people, and the greater the match between the perceived characteristics of an individual and the perceiver's prototype, the more likely the individual will be regarded as appropriate and effective in that position (Cantor & Mischel, 1979).

Violations of role prototypes precipitate impression management problems: relatively minor violations such as President Lyndon Johnson showing his surgical scar to photographers or Franklin Roosevelt cursing a stuck voting machine handle typically produce no more than a public outcry, but the disclosure of Gary Hart's relationship with a Miami model during the 1988 Presidential campaign doomed his bid for the Democratic nomination.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Leadership Images, Role Distance, and the Backstage of Restrooms
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena that is a negotiation tent ringed with armored vehicles and Apache helicopters where a stone-faced general faces Iraqi commanders, while on one wall a merry-go-round shows adults riding backwards with bored tolerance and a police officer arrests his own daughter; a door marked employees only opens onto a teacher's lounge where physicians joke about patients, a couple plans for an unruly guest, and two women in a bar restroom repair their makeup beside an executive washroom sign.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the question of how people survive the social context when norms and roles collide: hold up the leader's impression cards—competence as expert power, likeability through attraction power and the self-deprecating ROTC cadets, morality for presidents' families, potency under crisis from Roosevelt to Bush, and Schwarzkopf's stonelike intimidation—then walk the gauntlet of role distance on Goffman's merry-go-round and the menial chore done with sullenness, and the role conflicts of the police officer arresting his own daughter and the female executive trapped between the leader prototype and gender norms. Then enter the back region: Goffman's line about dropping the front, the teacher's lounge, the regressive jokes of physicians and waiters, the funeral home where the corpse is drained, stuffed, and painted, and the restroom as repair shop, staging area, and rank-segregated backstage.
key_concepts: Leaders throughout history have recognized that their effectiveness and power depends, in part, on their public images, and military officers, heads of state, corporate executives, and small group leaders alike must convey that they possess certain attributes and skills both to attain and to maintain their positions.

What we call leadership is actually an inference that we draw about certain individuals (Calder, 1977), so others' impressions determine in part who is and is not likely to become and remain a leader.

American Presidents, despite variations in their personal styles, typically try to appear presidential, that is, they try to match the public's prototype of a president however that is defined at a particular time in history (Hall, 1979).
The perception of competence is central to nearly every leader's effectiveness and is one source of a leader's influence, forming the basis of expert power (French & Raven, 1959).

Self-presentations of potency, being seen as powerful, calm, decisive, and in control, are particularly important when a leader's group is under stress: during World War II Franklin Roosevelt seemed to present a confident, if not cocky impression, during the Cuban Missile Crisis John Kennedy tried to be seen as calm, and during the Persian Gulf War of 1991 George Bush made a concerted effort to project an image of being controlled, unruffled, and unflappable.

Some leaders use self-presentations of intimidation, maintaining an appearance of impatience and hostility to threaten subordinates or enemies into submission and to exert coercive power (French & Raven, 1959), as General H. Norman Schwarzkopf did at the end of the Persian Gulf War when he arrived at negotiations ringed by armored vehicles and Apache helicopters and maintained a stonelike expression, refusing even a hint of a smile.

When people find themselves in a role that has the potential to cast undesirable aspersions on the images they want others to have, they use impression management to distance themselves from the role, showing others that they are not taking the role seriously, as seen in older children and adolescents who do not want their peers to see their parents treating them like a child.

People who are performing duties that they think are beneath them also use role distancing, doing a menial chore assigned by an employer with an obvious air of detachment, sullenness, or disgust, and Goffman (1961) demonstrated the behavior with a merry-go-round ride on which older children and adults ride with casual nonchalance, refusing to hold on to the pole, to show onlookers they do not take the ride seriously.

Self-presentational role conflict occurs when the public images required of one role are in opposition to those required of another role, such as a police officer who found his daughter among the people he was arresting in a drug bust, or when the self-presentational requirements of one's role conflict with self-presentational norms, as when female business executives must appear dominant and assertive to meet the leader prototype even though gender-related norms discourage women from being seen that way.

In the back region, away from the target, normal norm and role demands often do not apply, and the individual can relax, can drop his front, forego speaking his lines, and step out of character (Goffman, 1959).

When impression-relevant norms are suspended in back regions, people's behavior often takes on a regressive character: people tend to be excessively informal, status demarcations disappear, physicians joke among themselves about patients, teachers discuss topics in language that would shock their students, waiters display informality diners would find objectionable, and belching and flatulence may be regarded as funny rather than as breaches of decorum.

The backstage use of restrooms helps to explain why bathrooms are sometimes segregated by rank: executives use different washrooms than the rank-and-file, faculty use different restrooms than students, and officers use different latrines than enlisted soldiers, and even the segregation of restrooms by gender may serve as much a self-presentational as a biological function (Cahill et al., 1985).

assets.topic: Scrub the Appearance Ledger: Attractiveness, Cosmetics, Weight, and Sunbathing
assets.visual_frame_description: A time-scrubber playhead glides over a ledger page where an attractive and an unattractive stranger are rated side by side, passes a vanity table where a makeup compact causes a pimple to bloom and then spreads, pans across a surgical theatre with a face lift counter ticking to 75,000, a diet scale showing twice as many dieters as medical need, and ends at a beach where a tanner glows golden beside a melanoma statistics chart.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the chapter's opening ledger on physical attractiveness: how researchers find that attractive strangers are rated more positively on nearly every dimension, how everyday grooming and cosmetics are impression management, the cyclical trap of acne cosmetica, the millions of elective cosmetic surgeries, the stigma of overweight and the self-presentational reasons people diet, and the sunbathing paradox in which tanned people are judged more positively even though the incidence of malignant melanoma has quadrupled since 1960. Then weigh how each grooming choice reflects impression motivation rather than mere vanity.
key_concepts: Researchers have repeatedly found not only that we prefer to interact with attractive rather than unattractive people, but that we form more positive impressions of them.

When researchers compare people's ratings of attractive and unattractive strangers, attractive people are consistently perceived as more sociable, dominant, warm, mentally stable, intelligent, and socially skilled (Feingold, 1992).
From a self-presentational standpoint, anything that people do to make themselves more attractive to others reflects impression motivation.

Roughly one third of adolescent girls who regularly use makeup develop facial blemishes caused solely by the cosmetics, a condition known as acne cosmetica, which becomes cyclical because the makeup applied to cover blemishes in fact exacerbates the skin problem.

Over 1.5 million people undergo cosmetic surgery each year in the United States, and although some of this surgery repairs serious disfigurements, the vast majority is elective surgery intended simply to enhance the individual's appearance.

The primary reason women give for seeking breast augmentation is purely self-presentational: they want to look better to others and to reduce their self-consciousness over the size of their breasts (Birtchnell, Whitfield, & Lacey, 1990).
Eighty percent of people who seek orthodontic treatment do so for cosmetic reasons, not because they have difficulty chewing or talking (Giddon, 1983).

In contemporary America, being overweight is a stigma, and many people regard being overweight as aesthetically displeasing and draw negative inferences about overweight people, such as that they are lazy and self-indulgent.

Most people try to control their weight not because they want to be healthy per se but because they want others to regard them as attractive, and such self-presentational motives regarding weight may benefit many people.

Over twice as many people are on diets at any given time as need to diet for health reasons, and effects of unnecessary dieting include malnutrition, lack of energy, and increased susceptibility to disease.

The primary cause of skin cancer is excessive exposure to ultraviolet radiation from the sun or sunlamps, and the incidence of malignant melanoma, the form of skin cancer most likely to be fatal, has quadrupled since 1960.

Many people intentionally expose themselves to the sun because they think that being tanned will improve their appearance and lead to better impressions, and in fact tanned individuals are judged more positively than untanned ones.

assets.topic: Dialogue on Likability: Ingratiation, Similarity, Conformity, and the Impressions People Want
assets.visual_frame_description: A seminar table with Eddie Haskell's persona splitting in two, one sarcastic with the boys and one charming to Mrs. Cleaver, while a survey wall lists friendly, intelligent, attractive, and fun at the top and boring, conceited, and stupid at the bottom; a similarity meter glows as two faces align, and a campaign photo shows Bush playing horseshoes while a beer and a bag of pork rinds float beside him.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue about the most basic and ubiquitous self-presentational strategy, ingratiation: open with Eddie Haskell, who was sarcastic in the boys' room but charming to Beaver's parents, then work through the student survey of desired and undesired impressions, the gender differences in the top impressions, the potency of perceived similarity for liking, opinion conformity as the most common liking tactic, and the political uses of appearing similar, from middle-class politicians to George Bush's 1988 horseshoes and pork rinds campaign. Then debate the exceptions, including emphasizing dissimilarity to alienate and the backfiring of excessive conformity.
key_concepts: Leary opens with Eddie Haskell from Leave It to Beaver, who was sarcastic and impudent with the boys but charming and considerate when Beaver's parents walked in, illustrating that the faces we put on are determined by what we think the target will value.
Ingratiation, the strategy of conveying an impression of being likable, is perhaps the most basic and ubiquitous of all self-presentational strategies (Jones, 1990).
People who are liked and accepted reap a cornucopia of social rewards, including friendship, social support, companionship, help, romance, and status.

In a survey of students, most of the impressions they wanted to make involved attributes that would result in liking, such as being perceived as friendly, fun, sincere, funny, caring, and easy to talk to.
The impressions students did not want to make were ones that would lead others to dislike them, such as boring, conceited, obnoxious, superficial, self-centered, and mean.

Both men and women listed friendly, intelligent, attractive, and fun as their top four desired impressions, although consistent with sex role stereotypes women listed friendly first whereas men listed intelligent first, and neither wanted to be perceived as boring, conceited, or stupid.

One of the most potent determinants of liking is perceived similarity: in laboratory experiments, subjects' liking for a stranger is a direct function of how similar they think the stranger is to them (Byrne, 1971).

Conveying that one has similar opinions to a target, or opinion conformity, is perhaps the most common tactic people use when they want others to like them, and this is true not only in the United States but in other cultures as well.

Pressures to appear similar underlie a great deal of conformity, and politicians recognize this, wanting to be seen as middle class with middle-class values because voters prefer candidates whose positions are similar to their own.

During the 1988 presidential campaign, George Bush was photographed playing horseshoes rather than golf or tennis and mentioned he liked to unwind with a beer and a bag of pork rinds to counter the perception that he was out of touch with average Americans, though he dropped these presentations after being elected.

People may emphasize their dissimilarity from another person when their goal is to alienate or avoid that person or to show they are not easily swayed, and excessive opinion conformity may backfire if the person is perceived as insincere.

assets.topic: Audit Competence and Virtue: Self-Promotion, Playing Dumb, Effort, Exertion, and Exemplification
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger on a gym floor: a weight lifter strains under a barbell while a crowd of onlookers makes the plates heavier, a self-promoter's hot air balloon floats above a paradox stamp and a likability score that drops as competence rises, a woman feigns ignorance in front of a man, and a stooped exemplifier carries a virtue banner stamped honesty, dedication, and self-sacrifice while a hypocrisy stamp hovers nearby.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the chapter's competence and virtue accounts: check off self-promotion and its full range of behaviors, the self-promoter's paradox, and the likability-competence tradeoff, then ticket the ways people downplay effort to look able, refuse help to avoid seeming helpless, and play dumb to avoid chores, mislead opponents, or make others feel superior. Next, stamp effort and exertion: harder work when watched, social facilitation, social loafing and the football film trick, and close the ledger with exemplification and the three difficulties that face the self-presenter of virtue.
key_concepts: People who are viewed as knowledgeable and competent generally fare better within their social groups, tending to have higher status, exert more influence over others, and have better jobs.

Self-promotion is the tactic of trying to be perceived as competent, knowledgeable, or skilled, and people use a full range of behaviors to self-promote, not only verbal claims but also nonverbal behaviors and the staging of performances such as waiting until others are watching to perform a feat of skill (Jones & Pittman, 1982).

One primary reason that people try to do a good job on tasks is so others will perceive them as competent, and research has shown that people expend greater effort on tasks when the self-presentational stakes are high (Palmer, Welker, & Giacalone).

People who are afraid of being perceived as incompetent may reduce how hard they try so that a poor performance can be attributed to lack of effort rather than to low ability, as when subjects on an exercise cycle rated their effort lower alongside a rider who appeared to find the task easy.

The self-promoter's paradox is that, because people who are truly outstanding do not need to explicitly present themselves as competent, engaging in self-promotive self-presentations is often taken as evidence that the person is, in fact, not actually competent.

Self-promoters face a likability-competence tradeoff: even when it enhances others' perceptions of one's competence, self-promotion often causes others to like the person less, in part because people don't like others who brag.

People are reluctant to accept assistance from others if doing so implies that they are incompetent, helpless, or dependent, and they are more likely to accept help that is offered than to request it, because having to ask for help presents a greater self-presentational threat.

Approximately half of the women in studies published in 1950 and 1975 said they had pretended to be inferior to men, yet men were just as likely to play dumb as women, with men feigning inferiority in art more than women and women feigning intellectual inferiority more than men.

People play dumb to avoid onerous chores (if they minimize their competence, others won't ask them to do things), to make opponents underestimate their true ability, and to make the other person feel superior, and men may play dumb in front of their bosses more than women.

People work harder and exert more effort when other people are watching than when they are alone, and the self-presentational perspective suggests that the social facilitation effect occurs because people are motivated to make a good impression.

Social loafing occurs when people work in a group and their personal input is not clear, and the most effective way to reduce it is to make each individual's contribution public, which increases impression motivation, as when football coaches film every player on every play.

Exemplification involves self-presentations that convey an impression of virtue such as honesty, integrity, generosity, dedication, and self-sacrifice, and people are most likely to present such images when their targets value the virtue, as with clergy, dedicated employees, health-conscious people, and parents who present 'good' images to their children, yet exemplifying presentations must be supported by consistently exemplary behavior and cannot cross over into self-righteousness.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Specific Target Values, the Self-Presenter's Dilemma, Impression Importance, and the Multiple Audience Problem
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with four columns labeled TARGET VALUES, DILEMMA, IMPORTANCE, and AUDIENCES: a ROTC cadet flips from bragging to modest, a woman reshapes her self-image to fit a handsome man, an honest-dependable-friendly trait list towers over retiring and slipshod, and Grease's John Travolta stands between Olivia Newton-John and his roughneck buddies while eyes roll and tongues stick out as distancing signals.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a four-cell matrix of target-value mechanics: drop the ROTC cadets who self-enhanced when competence was scrutinized but turned modest when sociability mattered, and the women who conformed to a desirable man's preferences but ignored an undesirable man's, into TARGET VALUES; drop the self-presenter's dilemma and its three credibility tactics (balancing, secondhand presentations, and structuring the encounter so the target asks) into DILEMMA; drop the 300-trait importance ratings into IMPORTANCE; and drop the multiple audience problem, audience segregation, encoded messages, and distancing behaviors into AUDIENCES. Then close with the variation in which two targets value the same impression but it cannot be conveyed to both at once.
key_concepts: The chapter's guiding principle is that self-presentations are tailored to the perceived values and preferences of the target, so people convey different impressions of themselves to different targets and even to different classes of targets.

In one study, ROTC cadets who thought their competence at a decision-making task was under scrutiny presented themselves in a self-enhancing manner, but when they thought interpersonal ability was most important, they presented themselves more modestly (Gergen & Taylor, 1969).

In another study, women described themselves to a man whom they believed preferred either traditional or nontraditional women, and when the man was described in a socially desirable fashion they presented images consistent with the kind of woman they thought he liked (Zanna & Pack, 1975).

People sometimes present themselves differently to men and women because they assume men and women value different things, and both sexes are more willing to discuss behaviors consistent with their sex role with same-sex than other-sex friends.

The self-presenter's dilemma is that the more important it is for an individual to impress a target, the more likely the target is to be skeptical of the truthfulness of the individual's self-presentations.

One tactic people use to increase the credibility of their self-presentations is to balance them, such as conforming with another's opinion on important issues but disagreeing on trivial issues, so that their agreement may seem authentic rather than ingratiatory.

People can utilize secondhand self-presentations to skirt the dilemma because you are more likely to believe positive information about someone if you hear it from somebody else rather than directly from the person.

A person can structure the encounter so that the target asks about the attribute in question, because information presented in response to a question is less likely to be perceived as bragging or being manipulative.

In a study of 300 traits, the ten most important traits in describing what a person is really like were honest, dependable, friendly, loyal, reliable, responsible, self-confident, understanding, trusting, and selfish, and people should be highly motivated to control others' impressions on these dimensions.

The ten least important of the 300 traits were retiring, superstitious, commonplace, slow, formal, slipshod, hurried, quick, mild, and awkward, and in most cases people may be less concerned about how they are perceived on these dimensions.

Multiple audience problems arise when people find themselves wanting to present different impressions to two or more people in the same social encounter, and because they are so distressing, people usually work to avoid them through audience segregation, keeping different targets apart.

When audiences cannot be kept apart, people may send messages containing clues understood by one target but not another, or use distancing behaviors such as rolling the eyes, grimacing, or sticking out the tongue to communicate lack of commitment to a behavior they are performing.

assets.topic: Boss Level: The Boss' Illusion and the Experimenter as Target: Self-Presentational Biases in Research
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena that is a corner office where an employee mirrors the boss's casual posture and family photos while a shimmering illusion field shows the boss seeing a distorted, more-similar reflection of himself; on the other wall a psychology lab with a subject behind a one-way mirror inflating her self-description, a hypothesis-confirming questionnaire, and a researcher retreating behind a tape-recorded instruction while an anonymity stamp neutralizes the subject's motive.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the question of whether targets can ever trust what they see: stage the self-presentation matching effect, where a subject's favorable self-presentations make the other person describe themselves more favorably, and catch the target's failure to realize their own presentations caused the matching, taking the other person's modesty as low self-esteem. Then face the boss' illusion, in which employees mirror the boss's casual or devoted family image and the boss can't tell accuracy from flattery. Finally, confront the experimenter as target: subjects who answer to look adjusted or confirm the hypothesis, and the researcher's defenses of anonymity, concealed purpose, and self-removal from the setting.
key_concepts: In one study, subjects who were told to present themselves favorably caused the other person's subsequent self-descriptions to be more favorable than when subjects presented themselves unfavorably, a self-presentation matching effect that has been shown in other studies as well (Baumeister et al., 1989).

Subjects did not realize that the other person's self-descriptions had been influenced by their own positive or negative presentations, instead taking the other person's descriptions at face value and interpreting the other person's modesty as a sign of low self-esteem.

In businesses and work organizations, this effect is known as the boss' illusion: because employees sometimes present images they think the boss will value, bosses have no way to tell whether their impressions of employees are accurate or designed to please them.

If the boss is a devoted family person, employees may present themselves similarly, and if the boss comes across as casual and informal, employees may adopt a casual, informal image, so bosses often have the illusion that their employees are more similar to themselves than they really are.
Unless the employee is obviously sycophantic, the boss is unlikely to even question his or her impressions, so the boss' illusion persists in everyday organizations.

Unlike researchers in the natural sciences, researchers who study human behavior must deal with biases because, unlike atomic particles and viruses, subjects' actions may be influenced by their concerns with the experimenter's impressions and evaluations of them.

Most research subjects want to be perceived positively, as likeable, intelligent, competent, and psychologically adjusted, so they may not respond accurately to the researcher's questions if accurate answers might make the researcher form unfavorable impressions of them.

Some subjects try to make a good impression by looking cooperative and helpful, figuring out the study's hypotheses and responding in ways consistent with them, so the data will confirm the hypotheses whether or not they are actually true.

Researchers reduce the effects of subjects' self-presentational motives by assuring subjects their responses are fully anonymous, concealing the purpose of the study, and removing themselves from the experimental setting as much as possible with written or tape-recorded instructions.

Despite all of these precautions, researchers often worry that their results are contaminated by subjects' self-presentations, and when subjects convey impressions they think the researcher will value, the validity of the data is compromised.

assets.topic: Scrub the Constraints: What Others Know Binds the Images We Can Claim
assets.visual_frame_description: A playhead glides across a timeline of Nixon's post-Watergate years while a sandbox beach scene shows students inventing new hometowns and personalities; a laboratory panel displays the Schlenker experiment with 'others will know' versus 'no one will know' conditions, and a newsroom montage shows a scandalous photo contradicting a public denial.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through how the current social image constrains self-presentation: open on Nixon walking through the years after Watergate, trapped by a tainted image no protest could erase, then sit in on Leary's spring-break students who fabricated whole personas because nobody knew their histories. Run the Schlenker (1975) social sensitivity experiment, weigh the principle that people self-enhance unless others can check them, watch a self-presentational catastrophe unfold when a woman's nude photos contradict her claims, and close on why untrustworthy sources and close-knit villages tighten or loosen the bonds on the images we can claim.
key_concepts: As people construct their public identities, they take into account what people know or are likely to find out about them, so their current social images constrain the range of impressions they even try to make.

Knowing that he was widely regarded as a crook despite his protestations, Richard Nixon seemed to go out of his way to display attributes unrelated to the Watergate scandal, such as his extensive knowledge of foreign affairs.

Students who returned from spring break in Florida had fabricated new personas with new hometowns, families, colleges, and life histories, and even tried on different personalities, because their new acquaintances had no information to contradict them.

Typically, the impressions we try to make are constrained by the information that others have or are likely to get about us, and we usually find it very difficult to present ourselves in ways that are inconsistent with that information.

Our behavioral history constrains us to act as we have acted in the past, and once people have or are likely to obtain information about us, we recognize that the probability of making an alternative impression is low.

In Schlenker's (1975) experiment, subjects presented themselves consistently with how they had performed on the earlier test only when they thought the other group members would learn of their performance on the upcoming task.

Subjects who thought their later performance would not be known by the group presented themselves favorably regardless of how well they had performed on the test, leading Schlenker to observe that secret information known only to the individual can be ignored when selecting a public image.

People tend to present themselves in a self-enhancing way unless they think others have or are likely to obtain independent information that would contradict or discredit overly positive self-presentations.

When people misjudge what a particular target knows about them, the result is usually a full-fledged self-presentational catastrophe, because not only does the truth come to light but they come across as deceitful and manipulative.

A person whose self-presentational claims are blatantly discredited can rarely salvage the situation, as when a woman who indignantly denied she would ever pose nude was exposed by nude pictures a news reporter had obtained.

Even public information can be ignored if people believe that the target regards the source of the information as untrustworthy, such as when information is based on hearsay or comes from biased sources like one's enemies.

In a highly mobile society in which people's lives are private and quite segmented, people have considerable self-presentational freedom, but in close-knit societies where everyone knows everyone else, self-presentational constraints are much greater.

assets.topic: Dialogue on Successes, Failures and the Taxonomy of Predicaments
assets.visual_frame_description: A seminar table where one debater presents a laurel wreath with a sign reading MODESTY while the other shows a smugger's face labeled 'modesty backfire'; behind them a wall of four taxonomy cards, Individual Behavior, Interactive Behavior, Audience Provocation, and Bystander Behavior, each stamped with example scenes such as a dropped cafeteria tray, an awkward ex-lover meeting, and a joke that fell flat.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue between two speakers on the fate of images: one side argues that people whose successes are already known should stay modest, while the other side counters with the ways modesty backfires, from appearing nonchalant to seeming smug rather than humble. Then shift the debate to self-presentational failures: list the ways images get damaged, define the self-presentational predicament, and walk through Rowland Miller's four major categories of embarrassing circumstances, from individual behavior, normative public deficiencies, and abashed harm-doing to interactive, audience-provoked, and bystander embarrassment.
key_concepts: People who are sure that others already regard them positively typically refrain from trying to convey additional positive impressions of themselves and instead opt to convey an impression of modesty.

Subjects present themselves in a self-enhancing fashion when they think others are unaware of their successes but modestly if they think others know or will learn how well they have performed (Ackerman & Schlenker, 1975; Baumeister & Jones, 1978).

Not only do people respond favorably to slight modesty, but little is to be gained by trying to make an increasingly positive impression on those who are already impressed, and others are likely to form unfavorable impressions of people who trumpet their successes.

If others do not already hold a favorable impression of the person, they may take the person's modest self-presentational claims at face value, concluding that he or she is in fact not very good, or they may come to believe that the person is simply insecure.

Modest self-presentations may backfire if others interpret one's modesty as nonchalance, since shrugging off compliments may make one appear indifferent to others' opinions, and people may paradoxically interpret extreme modesty as a sign of arrogance (Pin & Turndorf, 1990).

Despite people's best efforts, things sometimes happen that threaten their images in others' eyes, such as a public failure, the discovery of previously secret information, out-of-character behavior, intentional humiliation, or failing to control one's body in ways that make a bad impression.

Events that clearly and sometimes irrevocably damage a person's image in others' eyes are called self-presentational predicaments, which are situations in which events have undesirable implications for the images people have claimed or desire to claim (Schlenker, 1980).
Rowland Miller (1992) asked university students to describe their last embarrassment, and analyses of these descriptions yielded four major categories of embarrassing circumstances.

Normative public deficiencies, one type of predicament caused by a person's own behavior, include physical pratfalls and inept performances, cognitive shortcomings, loss of control over one's possessions or body, and failures of privacy regulation.

Abashed harm-doing involves situations in which the person is embarrassed by harming others, such as breaking someone else's possession or spilling a drink on someone, and behaviors that lead to mere conspicuousness are embarrassing when people are the center of attention and don't know how to respond.

Interactive embarrassment includes awkward interactions in which people don't know what to say, such as meeting an ex-boyfriend or ex-girlfriend on the street, and team embarrassment in which the person was associated with other people who made a bad impression.

Nearly one fifth of the subjects in Miller's (1992) study described an audience-provoked predicament in which others divulged their secrets, made them the butt of jokes, or teased and insulted them, and empathic or vicarious embarrassment arises from simply witnessing another person's embarrassing actions.

assets.topic: Audit the Stigma Ledger: Marks, Concealment, Destigmatization, Compensation, Exploitation and Resignation
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger stamped with six columns, CONCEALMENT, ADMISSION, DESTIGMATIZATION, COMPENSATION, EXPLOITATION and RESIGNATION; a stamp with 'black is beautiful' presses onto a civil rights banner, a woman hides her condition behind a closed door, a man in a wheelchair reframes his scars as badges of honor, and a lab card shows menstruating women giving up on impressing a male interviewer.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit how people handle stigmas: open the ledger on the discrediting marks people carry, from past behaviors and physical characteristics to group membership and ancestry, then check off the six responses, concealment with its fear of detection, admission and destigmatization through denial or reframing, compensation on other dimensions, exploitation for sympathy, and resignation, closing with Kowalski and Chapple's study of menstruating women who gave up on impression management once the interviewer knew their condition.
key_concepts: A special type of predicament is created by the existence of a physical or psychological stigma, and most people possess certain characteristics that, if publicly known, might lead others to regard them as deviant, flawed, limited, or otherwise undesirable.

A mark becomes a stigma when it leads other people to draw negative inferences about the marked person's abilities, personality, characteristics, or desirability, and stigmatized individuals engage in a number of self-presentational tactics to minimize the impact of their stigma on others' reactions toward them.

People who try to conceal their marks often experience stress from the fear of detection, and when others find out about the mark they sometimes resent not having been told earlier, particularly if they are close friends (Jones et al., 1984).

One critical factor in gays' decisions to come out of the closet is accepting one's own homosexuality, yet in a study of gay men and lesbians the best predictor of openness was not self-acceptance but how respondents thought other people felt about homosexuals (Franke & Leary, 1991).

The simplest type of destigmatization is to deny that the mark should be regarded negatively, and by publicly downplaying the stigma a person can convey the impression of having grace in the face of adversity, sometimes using self-deprecating humor to show they have come to terms with their disabilities.

People seem to feel more justified acting negatively toward those whose stigma is perceived as controllable than toward those whose stigma is not controllable (Farina, Holland, & Ring, 1966; Rodin, Price, Sanchez, & McElligot, 1989).

A third type of destigmatization involves turning a stigma from a liability to a benefit, so physical limitations may be romanticized and injuries and scars obtained in battle may be worn like badges of honor.

Members of a stigmatized group sometimes work together toward destigmatizing themselves, as when the civil rights and black power movements sought not only equal rights but to destigmatize dark skin, exemplified in the phrase black is beautiful.

People who have a known stigma sometimes try to compensate for it by conveying more positive impressions of themselves on other dimensions, as shown when normal subjects who thought another person believed they were mental patients performed significantly better on skillful tasks (Farina, Allen, & Saul, 1968).

Stigmas involving physical or mental limitations are particularly susceptible to exploitation, since the marked person can advertise his or her condition to elicit sympathy, support, and other special treatment, or use the handicap to excuse other problems.

Stigmatized people may resign themselves to the fact that others regard them unfavorably, and such a realization often leads to self-presentational resignation, based on the reasoning that if a person cannot change others' views of the stigma, why bother worrying about what they think.

In Kowalski and Chapple's (1993) study of the stigma of menstruation, women who thought a male interviewer knew they were menstruating perceived that he liked them less and were less motivated to make an impression on him.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Saving and Repairing Face with Nonobservance, Apologies, Accounts and Compensation
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with four columns labeled NONOBSERVANCE, APOLOGIES, ACCOUNTS and COMPENSATION; a stomach rumbles unseen while everyone pretends not to notice, an apology scale slides from 'pardon me' to elaborate remorse, an account tree branches into refusals, excuses and justifications, and a lousy tennis player tells you about the marathon he ran while a cartoon team of image consultants maps post-game damage control.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a four-cell matrix of face-saving tactics: drop the studied nonobservance card into NONOBSERVANCE, sort apologies by severity and responsibility into APOLOGIES, file the accounts under REFUSAL, EXCUSE and JUSTIFICATION with every subvariant from pleas of ignorance and mitigating circumstances to minimization and principled justification, and place compensatory self-presentation in the COMPENSATION cell, closing with the athletes' damage-control cartoon and the cases where people avoid accounting altogether.
key_concepts: Sometimes people can save face by pretending that the predicament did not occur at all, applying this studied nonobservance to their own behavior, as when they do not indicate that it was their stomach that rumbled, or to the behavior of others, as when one pretends not to notice that someone else has stumbled (Goffman, 1955).

When people apologize, they accept responsibility for what they said or did while asking to be pardoned, and apologies and expressions of remorse are nearly always expected in predicaments that harm other people, so the failure to apologize exacerbates the person's self-presentational predicament.

The severity of a predicament is a function of two things: the more undesirable the impression that is created and the greater the person's apparent responsibility for the behavior that led to that impression, the more severe the predicament and the greater the person's embarrassment.

For most minor predicaments an apology alone will rectify the situation, because the apology shows that the person is not bad, was not intentionally hurtful, and, because he or she already regrets the behavior, does not need to be reprimanded or punished.

Schlenker and Darby's (1981) study showed that as severity increased, subjects were more likely to say they were sorry, express feelings of remorse, explicitly ask for forgiveness, and offer to help the victim, and even children as young as three years old evaluate transgressors who apologize more favorably than those who don't (Darby & Schlenker, 1982, 1989).

An account is a verbal explanation for unexpected, unacceptable, or unsatisfactory behavior that is designed to rectify a self-presentational predicament, and a person trying to account for his or her behavior has three general options: refusals, excuses, and justifications (Austin, 1956; Schlenker, 1980).

The ultimate account is a defense of innocence, also called a refusal, in which the person denies any and all responsibility for the event in question, and if others accept this type of account as valid, the person's predicament is resolved.

People use excuses to reduce their perceived responsibility for an undesirable event, and types of excuses include a plea of ignorance, mitigating circumstances such as being tired, under stress, drunk, or ill, and diffusion of responsibility in which the person argues the event was shared by a number of people.

Whereas people use excuses to minimize how responsible they appear for bad events, they use justifications to characterize their behavior as more appropriate, desirable, or defensible than it might at first appear, accepting personal responsibility but arguing the behavior was not really all that bad.

Justifications include direct minimization, claimed beneficence, comparative justification against worse actions, and principled justification such as victim derogation, in which people justify having hurt others by stressing that the victim deserved it, and victim benefaction, in which the action is claimed to have actually helped the person.

People can provide accounts that are either true or false, so excuses and justifications are not necessarily deceitful, and in some instances people think they can best protect their social images by avoiding giving an account altogether, such as dictators who claim invulnerability because of their power or people who use mystification, explaining that they cannot explain the reasons for their behavior.

When others have information about us that would contradict the impressions we want to make, we sometimes try to compensate for the negative impression by presenting particularly positive impressions on some other, unrelated dimension, as when a person who is known to be a lousy tennis player instead tells you about the marathon he ran, and when people face a self-presentational predicament because they violated some moral or legal code, they often go out of their way to do nice things for people, partly to repair their image in others' eyes (Tedeschi & Riordan, 1981; Apsler, 1975).

assets.topic: Boss Level: Embarrassment and the Nonverbal Display, From Blushing and Gaze Aversion to Nonhuman Appeasement
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena that is a crowded room where the player has just tripped: a blush meter rises red on the face while a fear gauge shows blanching on a frightened rival, spotlights zoom in on the three-element display of a red face, averted eyes, and a nervous grin, and behind it a chimp bares a full closed grin toward a dominant ape whose steady stare melts away as the animal wanders off.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the embarrassment display: face the feeling of mortification and chagrin, prove that embarrassment is not mere anxiety because embarrassed people blush while frightened people blanch, and defend the claim that embarrassment functions like physical pain in deterring us from harming our social well-being. Then walk the three-element display, facial blushing as a reaction to undesired social attention, gaze aversion, and the paradoxical nervous smile, and finish by dueling the evolution question, comparing the human display to the gaze aversion, full closed grin, and appeasement behaviors of chimpanzees and baboons.
key_concepts: The hallmark of making blatantly bad impressions is what we commonly call embarrassment, which is a feeling of mortification and chagrin that follows threats to one's public image, and people who are embarrassed feel awkward, flustered, self-conscious, and otherwise ill at ease (Parrott & Smith, 1991).

Embarrassment is clearly something other than intense anxiety per se, and part of the evidence is that embarrassed people often blush whereas when people are anxious or afraid, they do not blush, they blanch, because the sympathetic nervous system reduces blood flow to peripheral veins including those in the face, while embarrassed people show increased blood flow to the face paired with decreased blood flow to the extremities (Leary, Rejeski, Britt, & Smith, 1993).

Because people who make unfavorable impressions on others are derogated, ignored, shunned, punished, or ostracized, embarrassment may serve as a psychological mechanism that deters people from doing things that make the sorts of bad impressions that lead to rejection.

Embarrassment has the properties of a drive state that promotes efforts to maintain and repair one's social image, and the capacity for experiencing social discomfort may have evolved because people who were distressed about others' impressions were more likely to survive and reproduce than those who acted without regard for others' judgments, just as we would be unlikely to survive without pain to deter us from harming our physical well-being, we would be unlikely to survive without embarrassment to deter us from harming our social well-being (Baumeister & Tice, 1990; Miller & Leary, 1992).

When people encounter self-presentational predicaments, they tend to display a stereotypic set of nonverbal behaviors consisting of three primary elements that occur across various cultures: facial blushing, gaze aversion, and nervous smiling (Edelmann & Iwawaki, 1987).

Darwin concluded that blushing depends in all cases on a sensitive regard for the opinion, more particularly for the depreciation of others, and people also blush in response to being complimented, praised, or honored, when others scrutinize or stare at them, and even when others simply accuse them of blushing.

Contrary to the popular view, blushing is not simply a response to embarrassing predicaments but is a reaction to undesired social attention, so people do not blush in self-presentational predicaments because they are embarrassed or ashamed but because they are the objects of undesired social attention (Leary et al., 1992).

People who think they've made a bad impression on others tend to avert their gaze and avoid eye contact with other people, and when embarrassed, people find it difficult to meet the gaze of other people even if they want to (Edelmann, 1987; Modigliani, 1971).

The nervous smile of embarrassment is a silly, self-conscious grin that is paradoxical because embarrassed people rarely feel like smiling, and it is easily distinguished from a genuine smile of happiness or amusement because the eyes appear vacant rather than bemused (Asendorpf, 1990).

Human embarrassment displays are loosely analogous to the appeasement behaviors of other primates, since when facing a threat from a member of their own species, chimpanzees and baboons engage in behaviors that diffuse the threat, thereby avoiding aggression and maintaining the individual's position in the group.

Three aspects of nonhuman appeasement parallel human displays: a lower status primate invariably averts its eyes or looks obliquely at a dominant one, appeasement and submission involve a vacant, mirthless grin that Goodall (1988) called the full closed grin, and a steady gaze from a more dominant animal is a primary elicitor of appeasement behaviors.

Although there is no evidence that other primates blush, blushing and nonhuman appeasement share a common cause because people often blush when others stare at them, and obvious signs of embarrassment such as downcast eyes, nervous grinning, and blushing seem to placate other persons when the individual has performed behaviors that would otherwise result in unfavorable evaluations.

assets.topic: Scrub the Weakness Play: Supplication and the Art of Looking Helpless
assets.visual_frame_description: A playhead sweeps across a scene of a child exaggerating ineptitude at homework while a parent leans in to help; a ledger flips to the norm of social responsibility, then to a self-deprecator publicly mocked with praise bubbles but privately stamped with unfavorable verdicts, while a calendar ticks showing a resentment tracker climbing toward avoidance as a caption reads Supplication: Use Only as a Last Resort.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through supplication, the self-presentational strategy of advertising one's weakness and dependency to prompt others to nurture, protect, help, and care: how the norm of social responsibility obligates people to help those who cannot help themselves, how depressive feelings are sometimes shown or hidden depending on what the person wants, how preemptive self-deprecation fends off criticism, and how demonstrating incompetence or instability relieves people of onerous tasks. Then weigh the risks: the unflattering private opinions targets form of self-deprecators, the resentment and avoidance that eventually greet the chronically depressed, and why supplication is used only as a last resort.
key_concepts: The principle of complementarity states that one person's behavior will elicit a restricted range of behaviors from other people, so people can influence others to behave in certain desired ways by presenting particular impressions of themselves.
Supplication refers to self-presentations designed to make others regard the person as helpless in some regard, prompting others to nurture, protect, help, and care for them (Jones & Pittman, 1982).
By advertising their weakness and dependency, people can prompt others to nurture them, avoid onerous obligations, and excuse their own poor performance.

Because the norm of social responsibility says that people should help those who cannot help themselves, we often feel obligated to help those who need our assistance whether we really want to help them or not and to offer emotional support to those who are suffering.

Research suggests that people convey impressions of being sad and discouraged when they want others to come to their aid or when they want to avoid certain kinds of demands on them (Hill, Weary, & Williams, 1986).

Because social norms dictate that we should not attack or demean those who are inferior, publicly disparaging oneself should reduce the likelihood of criticism by others, so people sometimes preemptively self-deprecate to discourage others from criticizing them (Baumgardner, 1991).

By demonstrating their incompetence, weakness, ignorance, or instability, people may convince others that they are not capable of doing certain things, thereby relieving them of responsibility for doing so.
Even if the target of supplication offers help or emotional support, he or she may form an unflattering impression of the person as incompetent, weak, lazy, or insecure.
Although people often publicly support those who self-deprecate, they privately hold unfavorable opinions of them (Powers & Zuroff, 1988).

Over time, the target of supplication may feel trapped and resentful, begrudgingly coming to the supplicant's aid, and although people are generally happy to help a friend who is down, over time they begin to resent and avoid those who are often depressed (Segrin & Dillard, 1992).
Because supplication carries these risks, people probably use supplication only as a last resort (Jones & Pittman, 1982).
Researchers had a certain amount of difficulty getting subjects in their studies to self-deprecate even when doing so would have allowed them to avoid an onerous task (Kowalski & Leary, 1990).

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Sick Role: Playing Ill, Feigning Injury and Buying a Doctor's Excuse
assets.visual_frame_description: A split-stage debate: on one side a student calls in sick while a professor checks a doctor's note stamp, and on the other a hypochondriac's symptom counter climbs when a social intelligence test looms; an exhibit board titled THE SICK ROLE flips three cards, Exemption, Sub-Par Performance, Right to Care, while an injured claimant hesitates at the door of a chronic pain clinic marked Litigation Pending.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue on illness as a self-presentation: debate how most people have at some point feigned or exaggerated illness to escape unwanted duties, to excuse poor performance, or to collect nurturance, then walk the numbers, from the one-in-three college students who fraudulently claimed illness to the one-in-five workers who call in sick to rest. Then interrogate the sick role itself: the exemption from normal social and occupational obligations, the license to perform below one's normal ability, and the right to expect care, plus the hypochondriac's excuse for poor performance and the injured party's stake in staying hurt until litigation ends. Close with illness validation, physician legitimation, and the reverse side, self-presentations of healthfulness.
key_concepts: Most people have at one time or another feigned or exaggerated illness or injury to get out of something they didn't want to do, to account for undesirable behavior, or to elicit nurturing responses from other people.

In a survey conducted at a major northeastern university, an average of one out of three students reported that they had fraudulently claimed they were ill while in college, usually to gain more time for a test or assignment (Caron, Whitbourne, & Halgin, 1992).

One study found that one out of five American workers calls in sick at least once a year because they really need time to rest and relax, and this tactic may actually increase worker productivity in the long run because workers who don't relieve stress may perform less efficiently and may even really get sick (Siegel, 1993).

The sick role is a set of culturally-shared assumptions about people who are ill, and because it stipulates that people who are ill or injured are exempt from normal social and occupational obligations, appearing sick can be used to avoid onerous activities or duties (Gordon, 1966; Parsons, 1951).

The sick role also includes the assumption that people cannot be expected to perform up to their normal levels of ability when they are ill, so self-presentations of illness can be used to excuse poor performances in class, in athletics, at work, and even in social life.

Because their poor health, whether real or imagined, can serve as an excuse for poor performance, hypochondriasis can protect people from evaluation apprehension, and for some people appearing to be in poor health has social and personal benefits (Rezek & Leary, 1991).

In one study, subjects who scored high on a measure of hypochondriasis reported having a greater number of physical symptoms when they thought that their score on a test of social intelligence might be affected by their health, whereas hypochondriacs who took a nonthreatening test did not overemphasize their symptoms (Smith, Snyder, & Perkins, 1983).

A third aspect of the sick role is that sick individuals have a right to expect others to help care for them, so letting other people know you are sick is likely to elicit concern and nurturance (Gordon, 1966).

In personal injury cases, people have a stake in continuing to seem injured until their legal claim is resolved, which is why some chronic pain clinics refuse to admit accident victims to their programs until litigation is over (Weissman, 1990).

Because we all realize that others may fake or exaggerate illness, we often require independent validation of a person's illness, and the most widely accepted validation is legitimization by a physician, with a doctor's excuse widely accepted as evidence that a person is ill (Gordon, 1966).

Even if the physician can't find anything wrong, a trip to the doctor's office shows other people that the person truly didn't feel well, and people who claim to be sick and go to a doctor are perceived to be more ill than people who only claim to be sick.

People who really are ill or injured sometimes want others to think they are not, and self-presentations of healthfulness may contribute to illness when people who are ill or injured fail to take proper care of themselves so that others don't detect their medical problem.

assets.topic: Audit the Craziness Claim: Feigned Madness, Schizophrenic Impression Managers and Faked Test Answers
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger stamped PSYCHOPATHOLOGY OR PERFORMANCE: exhibit cards slide in showing a courtroom insanity plea, a field being sown with salt, Corporal Klinger in a dress, and two interview rooms where the same patient appears calm for the open ward and disturbed for the release hearing; beside them a stack of questionnaires, one signed and inflated with socially desirable answers, with a stamp reading This Is Also Self-Presentation.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit how people manage impressions of psychological stability and instability: check off the insanity plea, Berkowitz's admitted fabrication of demons and talking dogs, Odysseus sowing his field with salt to dodge the draft, and Klinger's dresses in M*A*S*H, then open the Braginsky and Braginsky ledger on schizophrenics who displayed more or less symptomatology depending on whether they wanted an open ward or a release from the hospital. Cross-check the replicated findings, Watson's caution that patients suppress abnormality rather than fake psychoticism, and then stamp the personality inventories: self-report as self-presentation, faking good versus faking bad, the Marlowe-Crowne scale's 33 items, and the discovery that people even fake the faking scale when they sign their names.
key_concepts: Defendants accused of heinous crimes often plead not guilty by reason of insanity, hoping that they will be sent to a psychiatric institution rather than to prison.

Legal and medical experts have been discussing the problem of feigned insanity at least since the 18th century, and as early as 1806 defendants have successfully faked mental illness to avoid conviction (Geller, Erlen, Kaye, & Fisher, 1990).

In the case of the Son of Sam murders, David Berkowitz openly admitted that he feigned mental illness, later saying he made up the demons and talking dog to find some form of justification for his criminal acts against society.

People have tried to convince others they were crazy to avoid military service even in ancient times, and in The Odyssey, to avoid serving in the war with Troy, Odysseus sowed a field with salt, purposefully trying to appear crazy.

Some have argued that what appear to be symptoms of psychological problems are sometimes self-presentational strategies designed to accomplish certain interpersonal goals, though many people do experience severe emotional and behavioral problems over which they have little or no control.

In a classic study by Braginsky and Braginsky (1967), 30 long-term schizophrenics in a mental hospital were interviewed by a staff psychologist, and the patients were found to display either more or less psychotic symptomatology depending on their goals.

Patients who thought they were being evaluated for the open ward displayed significantly fewer indications of psychological problems than those who thought their suitability for release was being assessed, describing themselves more positively and reporting fewer medical and psychological problems.

No patient who thought he or she was being evaluated for the open ward reported any severe problems, whereas half of those in the other condition did so, and psychologists judged the open-ward patients as exhibiting less psychopathology and requiring less supervision.

The finding that diagnosed mental patients selectively present themselves as more or less disturbed depending on which image will most benefit them has been replicated by other researchers, and the psychiatric literature contains case studies of people who appear severely disturbed but are managing their impressions to appear dysfunctional (Fontana & Gessner, 1969; Watson, 1972).
Watson (1973) suggested that such patients are more likely to suppress impressions of abnormality when normalcy will result in desired outcomes than they are to actually fake psychoticism.

Some have suggested that some of the underprivileged use mental institutions as a resort, and as Ludwig and Farrelly (1967) observed, schizophrenics are more expert at producing certain reactions on the part of the staff, family, and society at large than the latter are at evoking desired patient responses.

Because self-report measures of personality simply ask respondents to describe themselves by answering a series of questions, taking a psychological test is a form of self-presentation that is not notably different from self-presentation in social interactions (Hogan & Jones, 1983).

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Intimidation, Countertoughness and the Retaliation Grid
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with four columns labeled TOUGH IMAGE, COMPLIANCE, NEGOTIATION and VIOLENCE; cards fly in showing a schoolyard bully, a child's tantrum in a supermarket, a negotiator pounding a table while constituents watch, and a prisoner starting an unprovoked fight; a side panel runs a retaliation spiral of escalating arrows while a bystander counter ticks up and a caption reads Sticks and stones may break my bones, but insults escalate.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a four-cell matrix for intimidation: drop the tough-guy image cards into LOOKING TOUGH, the power imbalance between teachers and students, employers and employees, sergeants and recruits, and the make-a-scene threat of the powerless into COMPLIANCE, the negotiator's tough front, the audience effect on constituents, and the countertoughness response into NEGOTIATION, and the unprovoked fights of self-image promoters, the 50 groups claiming the World Trade Center bombing, and the police raid's display of force into VIOLENCE AS IMPRESSION. Then run the retaliation column: insults as unfavorable impressions, gang honor, the conflict spiral, Goffman's winner, and why retaliation peaks when bystanders are watching.
key_concepts: Realizing that a person willing to forego others' good will and to live with the reputation of being nasty can get others to do what he or she wants, people sometimes foster an intimidating, threatening image to induce others to do their bidding (Jones & Pittman, 1982).

The schoolyard bully, the gruff boss, and the stern parent may all be fostering images that elicit others' unquestioning compliance, with the bully relying on an image of physical violence and the gruff boss on being socially unpleasant.

Usually self-presentational intimidation is used by persons with the greater power in an interaction, such as teachers intimidating students, employers employees, and sergeants recruits, and people hesitate to direct intimidating self-presentations toward those who have the power to retaliate.

Persons with less power can often get others to do what they want by threatening to make a scene, as children do when they throw tantrums in public places, and as patients in mental institutions do by being difficult with the staff.
Many negotiators believe that by appearing tough and uncompromising they will lower their opponents' aspirations and discourage them from asking for too much (Wall, 1991).
Research shows that negotiators work harder to look tough when the parties on whose behalf they are negotiating are present (Carnevale, Pruitt, & Britton, 1979).

The complementary response to intimidation, toughness, and dominance is often countertoughness rather than submissiveness, so negotiators often avoid this strategy when their opponent has the resources to retaliate.
In order for physical intimidation to succeed, people must occasionally back up their threatening posture with real aggression, and much seemingly senseless violence may serve this purpose.

Senseless, unprovoked aggression may be more effective self-presentationally than justified aggression because it shows that the aggressor is clearly not a person to be trifled with, and bullies tend to pick on their victims in relatively public settings where their peers can see.

Toch (1992) found that one out of four of the violent men he studied used violence to promote his self-image, working hard at manufacturing the impression that he is formidable and fearless, with fights designed as demonstration matches to impress the victim and the audience.

An extreme and unusual instance of self-presentational intimidation occurs when militant groups claim responsibility for attacks that they didn't commit, and after the World Trade Center bombing in 1993 more than 50 groups called to claim responsibility to establish that they are a force to be reckoned with.

Not all self-presentational intimidation is bad, because people may adopt an intimidating persona simply to ward off possible attacks, and police conducting raids on dangerous suspects shout commands, use physical force, and brandish weapons to convey an intimidating impression of strength and forcefulness (Felson & Tedeschi, 1993).

assets.topic: Boss Level: Retaliatory Aggression, Sexual Signals, Modeling and the Career Climb
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena shaped like a spiral staircase: at the base a conflict spiral of reciprocal insults climbs past gang colors, through a party where a man misreads a hand-hold, past a Gettysburg ridge where a general strolls smoking a cigar, to an office tower where a desk displays a CONFIDENTIAL folder and a Wall Street Journal while a raise graph ticks upward; a caption reads Conveying Certain Impressions Leads to Predictable Reactions.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the full range of instrumental self-presentation: survive the retaliation gauntlet where insults are attacks on one's public image, where gang honor is defended, where ignoring an insult worsens the damage, where Goffman's winner out-handles the adversary, and where retaliation flares hottest when third parties watch and conflict spirals escalate. Then run the seduction corridor of subtle, deniable sexual cues, the male threshold for reading sex into mundane behaviors, and the 39 percent of women who said no while meaning yes, and finish on the career ladder: role modeling parents, Schurz's cigar at Gettysburg, image consultants, the confidential folders and Wall Street Journal props, outside job offers, fake affection for the boss, and Gould and Penley's finding that self-presenters get raises.
key_concepts: People are particularly likely to retaliate aggressively when others insult or demean them or, in self-presentational terms, when others indicate that they hold highly unfavorable impressions of them, and the most common cause of aggression among street gangs is a perceived insult to the honor of a gang or one of its members (Felson, 1978, 1982; Horowitz & Schwartz, 1974).

Failing to respond to an insult often causes further damage to the person's image, conveying that he or she is weak, afraid, or simply unable to come up with an appropriate reaction, whereas by retaliating the offended party can reestablish that he or she is a forceful and assertive person who cannot be treated with disrespect.
