As Goffman (1967) observed, in aggressive interchanges the winner not only succeeds in introducing information favorable to himself and unfavorable to others, but also demonstrates that as an interactant he can handle himself better than his adversaries.

Because retaliation casts the insulter in a negative light, the original provocateur is inclined to respond to the counterattack, and unchecked these reciprocal attacks can escalate into a conflict spiral.

People are most likely to retaliate against insults when third parties are present, particularly if they know that the bystanders value aggression, suggesting that aggressive retaliation is performed as much for the benefit of bystanders as for the insulter (Bond & Venus, 1991).

Toch (1992) identified people who are unusually sensitive to real or imagined attacks upon their public images as self-image defenders, whose violence arises in the form of responses to challenges, retaliations to slights, or reactions against aspersions to his advertised self-conception.

Because norms discourage people from explicitly conveying their sexual interest in people they do not know well, people often use subtle behaviors to express their sexual interest that can be denied if the other person takes offense, making the conveying of sexual intent a tricky affair of subtle, often ambiguous cues (Grammer, 1990).

Men and women sometimes interpret nonverbal behaviors differently, with men having a lower threshold for perceiving behaviors sexually, and in Kowalski's (1993) study, when the behaviors were more mundane such as having a drink or holding hands, men were more likely to infer sexual interest than the women.

Muehlenhard and Hollabaugh (1988) found that 39 percent of the women they surveyed reported saying no to a man's sexual advances when they really meant yes, with a primary self-presentational reason being the fear of appearing promiscuous, and such a self-presentation is risky because it may lead men to disregard what a woman says when she really means no (Kowalski, 1992).

A great deal of research over the past 30 years has demonstrated that role modeling is one of the most potent ways to influence other people's behavior, since people often imitate what they see other people doing, and most parents try to present themselves to their children in a somewhat idealized fashion so the child will develop socially desirable patterns of behavior.

During the American Civil War, afraid that his men would retreat under the Southern artillery barrage at the Battle of Gettysburg, Brigadier General Carl Schurz walked calmly up and down the ranks smoking a cigar to model bravery, and military leaders have been killed when they purposefully took cover in a leisurely fashion so as not to appear hasty or concerned to their soldiers (Linderman, 1987).

Many people believe that merit alone is not sufficient to be hired and promoted, so it is essential to convey an image of being competent, powerful, and effective, and Gould and Penley (1984) found that employees who used self-presentation as a career strategy by making supervisors aware of their accomplishments or presenting themselves as people who get things done received more frequent salary increases than those who did not.

assets.topic: Scrub the Self Engine: Self-Reflection, the Self-Concept and the Phenomenal Self
assets.visual_frame_description: A playhead sweeps across a mirror in which a child under age two looks blank while a chimpanzee squints at its own reflection, then across a pub scene where a beer glass ticks down the drinker's self-awareness and manners become automaton gestures; a ledger flips open titled SELF-CONCEPT listing body, personality, relationships, roles, beliefs, history, possessions, while a spotlight beam narrows to a thin bright slice labeled PHENOMENAL SELF as a caption reads Only What You Think About You, Moves You.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the machinery of the private self: the capacity for self-reflection (Mead's self-reflexivity) that lets people think consciously about themselves, how the self got banished from behavioral science and revived by humanistic psychologists and the past 25 years of self-process research, and how a person without an active self cannot deliberately impression-manage. Then walk the boundary lines: why children under two can't consciously self-present, why intoxicated people stop worrying about how they come across, how manners and grooming harden into habitual self-presentation, how the self-concept stores beliefs about bodies, traits, relationships, roles, beliefs, histories and even possessions, how it works as a theory that interprets experience, and why only the slice of the self-concept in conscious awareness, the phenomenal self, actually drives behavior.
key_concepts: The self is the cognitive structure that allows people to think consciously about themselves, and when we say a person has a self we simply mean that he or she has the capacity for self-reflection, or what Mead (1934) called self-reflexivity.

Without a self we could not consciously plan for the future, worry about personal problems that were not immediately present, agonize over past misfortunes, consciously consider alternatives, think about death, or even recognize ourselves in a mirror.

Research evidence suggests that, with the exception of certain great apes such as chimpanzees, other animals do not have the ability to consciously contemplate themselves, and even lower monkeys cannot learn to recognize their own reflections in a mirror (Gallup, 1977).

A person without a self, or one whose self was not currently active, could not consciously impression-manage, and young children do not develop the capacity for deliberate self-presentation until their self begins to develop, usually after age two (Buss, 1980; Lewis, Sullivan, Stanger, & Weiss, 1989).
The fact that alcohol seems to interfere with self-reflection helps to explain why people who are intoxicated don't worry as much about how they're coming across as they normally do (Hull, 1981).

Although a person must be self-aware to engage in deliberate impression management, certain self-presentational behaviors may be performed so frequently that they become habitual and no longer require self-awareness, and many manners fall into this category of behavior (Schlenker, 1980).

The self-concept consists of the set of beliefs that a person holds about him- or herself, including beliefs about our physical bodies, our personal characteristics, our social relationships, the roles we play, the beliefs we consciously hold, our personal histories, and even our possessions.

The self-concept has been compared to a person's theory about what he or she is like (Epstein, 1973), and like a theory it contains not only facts that we believe are true about ourselves but also untested hypotheses about how we would respond in new situations.

The self-concept is used to interpret experiences, so two people with different self-theories may interpret the same event differently, as when an intelligent student attributes a poor grade to the teacher's unfairness while another takes it as a reflection on his or her intelligence.

The phenomenal self is the portion of one's self-beliefs that is present in conscious awareness at any particular time (Rhodewalt, 1986), and it includes both contents of the self-concept being thought about at the moment and thoughts about momentary states such as being tired.

People tend to behave consistently with their internal attitudes, morals, and self-concepts only when they are thinking about themselves and the phenomenal self is activated, whereas when people are blocked from thinking about themselves they often behave very uncharacteristically (Diener, 1980).

The images people convey to others are likely to be affected by whatever is in the phenomenal self at a given time, and the parts of oneself that are not part of the phenomenal self will not be represented in one's self-presentations to others.

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Honest Front: Tactical Truth, Legibility, and the Two Flavors of Self-Esteem
assets.visual_frame_description: A courtroom split stage: on one side an accuser holds a mask labeled PRETENSE, while the defendant projects slides of an honest résumé and a man deliberately smiling wider to make his joy legible; the witness stand displays two report cards of C students, one smiling, one deflated, and a gauge swinging between TRACKED through situations (state) and steady across years (trait), with a scale labeled LOW SELF-ESTEEM actually resting on MODERATE.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue defending self-presentation against the charge of inherent deceit: rebut Buss and Briggs' 'pretense' objection and Bednar's 'pretending' accusation with the finding that self-presentations are as likely to be accurate and honest as deceptive. Then interrogate why honest people must be tactical: behavior constrained by roles and norms reveals little, emotional expressions need 'legibility,' and time runs out, so people selectively present information that is essentially true. Cross-examine self-esteem next: Coopersmith's definition of evaluation and worth, why two C students with the same self-concept can feel differently, the consistency of trait self-esteem versus the fluctuation of state self-esteem, and why calling anyone's self-esteem truly 'low' is really a misnomer.
key_concepts: Without denying that people sometimes present public images that are inconsistent with how they see themselves, their self-presentations are as likely to be accurate and honest as they are to be deceptive and duplicitous (Schlenker, 1980; Tetlock & Manstead, 1985).
People often consciously and deliberately manage their impressions so that other people will see them as they see themselves (Gergen, 1968; Jones & Pittman, 1982).

The primary reason people sometimes must deliberately behave to disclose information about themselves is that other people often cannot infer much about us simply from observing our behavior, which is so constrained by the roles we play and the norms of the situation that it reveals little personal information about us.

Even when our behavior could potentially convey something about us, people sometimes exaggerate their emotional expressions to increase the legibility of their reactions, assuring that others accurately decipher what they are feeling (DePaulo, 1992).

Because people do not have unlimited time to disclose information about themselves, they must select which information to emphasize, so self-presentation often involves selectively presenting information about oneself that is essentially true (Schlenker & Weigold, 1992).

The self-concept provides a subjective indicator of the likelihood that we will be able to successfully project a particular image, and in most cases we are more likely to successfully convey impressions that are consistent with our self-concepts than impressions that are not.

Because failing to successfully present a particular image is often worse than not trying in the first place, believing that one lacks the ability to make a particular impression may deter people from trying to do so.

Self-esteem refers to a person's evaluation of him- or herself, and Coopersmith (1967) defined it as the evaluation the individual makes and customarily maintains with regard to himself, expressing an attitude of approval or disapproval and indicating the extent to which the individual believes himself to be capable, significant, successful, and worthy.

Whereas the self-concept involves beliefs or thoughts about oneself, self-esteem refers to the person's evaluations and feelings about those beliefs, so two people with the same self-concept may have different self-esteem, as when one C student feels very good about being a C student while another's self-esteem is deflated by that fact.

People show some degree of consistency in how they evaluate themselves across different situations and over time, and a person's general, characteristic level of self-esteem is called trait self-esteem.

The term low self-esteem is really a misnomer because very few people can be accurately described as having truly low self-esteem, most people rate themselves as neutral or better, and so-called low self-esteem people are really moderate in how they evaluate themselves (Tice, 1993).

A person's level of self-esteem in a particular situation at a particular time is called state self-esteem, and people's evaluations of themselves fluctuate as they go from one situation to another, as when a student feels low self-esteem in gym class but very good about herself in algebra class.

assets.topic: Audit the Motivation Ledger: State Hits, Trait Profiles, and the Acquisitive-Protective Ledger
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger with three columns: STATE, TRAIT, and CONFIDENCE. Under STATE, a test-taker's score plummets then climbs as he presents himself to an interviewer who will reveal his evaluation, but stays flat when feedback is sealed; under TRAIT, a balance scale tips between a trophy marked ACQUISITIVE and a shield marked PROTECTIVE while a questionnaire shows a respondent hedging to the middle boxes; under CONFIDENCE, a high self-esteem figure strides into a spotlight while a low self-esteem figure shrinks from a pre-formed negative file marked DO NOT DISCONFIRM.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit the two links between self-esteem and self-presentation: differing motives and differing confidence. Trace the need to maintain self-esteem and approval-seeking, then audit Schneider's 1969 experiment where low scorers expecting interviewer feedback self-enhanced while lows expecting no feedback did not. Cross-check the trait side: self-verification motives that make even negative self-views worth confirming, Swann's preference for negative feedback on unfavorable attributes only, and Baumeister, Tice, and Hutton's resolution that high self-esteem people pursue acquisitive self-presentation while low self-esteem people pursue protective self-presentation. Then stamp the confidence column: why self-esteem scales really measure self-presentation, why the low self-esteem endorse middle-of-the-road noncommittal answers, and why highs take bigger self-presentational risks while lows refuse to disconfirm others' negative impressions.
key_concepts: People have a basic need to maintain their self-esteem, that is, to evaluate themselves positively and to feel good about themselves, and as a result they do a great many things to maintain and enhance their self-esteem, some of which involve self-presentation (Brown, 1993; Leary & Downs, in press; Steele, 1988).

Because their feelings of worth are based partly on others' evaluations of them (Cooley, 1902; Shrauger & Schoeneman, 1979), people may seek others' approval as a way of increasing low self-esteem and/or maintaining high self-esteem, and presenting particular desirable impressions is one way of gaining approval (Jellison & Gentry, 1978).

In Schneider's (1969) experiment, subjects who received low scores on an important-ability test and expected the interviewer's evaluation to be revealed to them presented themselves more positively and conveyed more positive impressions than low scorers who did not expect feedback, because their self-presentations would enhance their damaged self-esteem only if they received the interviewer's evaluation.

People sometimes want self-verifying feedback from others, feedback that is consistent with how they see themselves, because receiving feedback that is discrepant from one's self-concept can be unsettling, implying that the person does not really know him- or herself very well.
As surprising as it may seem, research shows that people do attempt to verify their self-views, even if those views are negative (Swann, 1983, 1987).

Swann, Pelham, and Krull (1989) showed that people prefer positive feedback over negative feedback regardless of their level of self-esteem, but when dealing only with attributes on which they regard themselves unfavorably, people prefer to receive negative feedback.

Baumeister, Tice, and Hutton (1989) suggested that people with high self-esteem are primarily motivated to make favorable impressions, called acquisitive self-presentation, whereas people with low self-esteem are motivated to avoid making unfavorable impressions, called protective self-presentation (Arkin, 1981; Tice, 1992).

As Baumeister et al. (1989) put it, low self-esteem entails a self-presentational orientation based on protecting oneself from failure, embarrassment, rejection, and humiliation, whereas high self-esteem entails a self-presentational orientation based on enhancing one's prestige and reputation for competence.

Scores on standard measures of trait self-esteem more directly measure self-presentation than the person's own self-evaluations per se, because the way that people score high on self-esteem scales is by indicating that they possess desirable attributes or otherwise feel positively about themselves.

People concerned about failure and embarrassment would be expected to describe themselves in an average, middle of the road, noncommittal manner, not too good and not too bad, which is precisely what people with so-called low self-esteem do, since endorsing positive attributes is risky and endorsing negative attributes makes a bad impression.

Persons high in self-esteem take greater self-presentational risks than those low in self-esteem, and Schlenker, Weigold, and Hallam (1990) found that high self-esteem persons became more self-aggrandizing as social evaluative pressures increased while low self-esteem persons became more self-presentationally cautious under such circumstances.

Baumeister (1982b) found that persons high in self-esteem were more likely than lows to try to counteract negative information that other people had about them, whereas persons with low self-esteem appeared reluctant to try to disconfirm others' preexisting impressions, presumably because they doubted they could successfully refute them.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: The Desired-Unwanted Grid and the Dilemma Collision Table
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with columns labeled DESIRED SELF (a patient parent, a fit athlete) and UNDESIRED SELF (a shamed slacker, a feared failure) with arrows showing every presented image drifting toward one column and away from the other; a central collision table shows five converging beams meeting in one easy spotlight, then two beams clashing to spark a DILEMMA marker over four vignettes: a student facing a grouchy teacher, a couple at a ballpark, an interview desk with a computer, and a break room where a sexist joke lands, with a caption reading When What You Are Clashes With What You Can Win.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a four-cell matrix of the private self in action: drop cards for the person you want to be into DESIRED SELF, the person you never want to become into UNDESIRED SELF, and Markus and Nurius' possible selves plus Ogilvie's dreaded selves into the note that people's self-presentations lean toward the desired and away from the undesired. Then run the collision table: when the self-concept, the desired self, the roles and norms, the target's values, and the existing image all converge, impression management is easy, but when any pair collides, a self-presentational dilemma erupts. Place the classics on the grid: the student who disagrees with a grouchy teacher, the sports fan whose date hates sports, the applicant quizzed on computers, and the egalitarian hearing sexist jokes, and end on the principle that self-aware, honest presenters are steered by the phenomenal self, self-esteem, and desired and undesired selves.
key_concepts: The ideas of what we would and would not want to become are called our desired and undesired selves (Markus & Nurius, 1986; Ogilvie, 1987).

The term ideal self is misleading because it suggests that people strive to achieve some lofty, if not unreachable, state of being, whereas in reality most of us are more reasonable than to strive for our ideal self.

Just as impression management is affected by people's beliefs about the kinds of people they are, it is also affected by their perceptions of the kinds of people they want to be, and even when they are trying to be accurate, people's self-presentations tend to lean in the direction of their desired selves and away from their undesired selves (Leary & Kowalski, 1990; Schlenker, 1985).

People's desired and undesired selves presumably reflect their own values, and when people value certain characteristics they usually want to convey to others that they possess those characteristics, so a person who values patience will manage impressions to convey an image of patience.

Impression management can be used to actually help the person move closer to his or her desired self, because when people successfully present a particular image of themselves to others they sometimes begin to internalize that image (Baumeister, 1982a; Tedeschi & Norman, 1985).

Research shows that people who are induced to describe themselves as extraverted not only later rate themselves as more extraverted but actually behave in a more outgoing fashion in subsequent interactions (Fazio, Effrein, & Falender, 1981; Tice, 1992).

The principle of the private self holds that when people are self-aware and not motivated to deceive others, their self-presentations are influenced by their phenomenal self (and, thus, self-concept), self-esteem, and desired and undesired selves.

The ideal social encounter, from an individual's self-presentational perspective, is one in which all factors point the person toward constructing the same image, as when the self-concept, desired self, roles and norms, the target's values, and the person's existing image in others' eyes all converge toward the same image.
A self-presentational dilemma arises when two or more of these factors point to different impression-management tactics, particularly if the desired images are mutually exclusive.

One of the most common and personally troubling self-presentational dilemmas occurs when the image that would have the desired effect on a target is discrepant from the person's own self-concept, as when an individual recognizes that he or she does not possess attributes that the target values or possesses qualities the target will view negatively.

Everyday life is replete with such dilemmas: a student disagrees with a grouchy teacher, a sports fan finds that her date hates sports, a job interviewer asks about the applicant's familiarity with computers, and a sexual egalitarian's co-workers start telling sexist jokes.

In such dilemmas, an entirely truthful self-presentation that is consistent with the person's self-concept would likely result in a less positive impression and less favorable social or material outcomes than a presentation tailored toward the target's values, yet most of us are so socialized to be truthful that we have difficulty telling bold-faced lies about ourselves.

assets.topic: Boss Level: Authentic, Deceptive and Exclusionary Resolutions, Then the Self That Rewrites Itself
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena shaped like a gated fortress: at the gate three doors labeled AUTHENTIC, DECEPTIVE, and EXCLUSIONARY, where a hand slides cards out of a deck while a secret vault seals behind it; inside, a portrait of Machiavelli presides over a negotiation table where a high Mach's lie is stamped UNDETECTED and children coax others toward quinine crackers while observers note them honest; at the summit, a self-portrait redraws itself under four dials labeled CHOICE, LATITUDE, PUBLICNESS, AFFIRMATION, while a figure acting depressed sinks into a fog and another in an inflated mask wonders why no one's applause feels real, with a caption reading Present It, And You May Become It.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the full arc of the private self: first run the dilemma gauntlet where people resolve clashes either authentically (forced by discrediting information or held as a matter of principle), deceptively (stretching from white lies to absolute fabrications, gated by the seriousness of the deception, the odds of detection, and the incentive), or exclusionary-evasively (withholding self-relevant cards, as the Lamphere and Leary extraverts hid their extraversion from introvert-loving targets, and as personal secrets about indiscretions, traumas, and failures hide the self). Then confront the Machiavellian cadre: the scale, the utilitarian view of interactions, the quinine-cracker children rated honest while lying, and the high Machs who negotiate, resist pressure, and lie undetected. Finally, clear the internalization sanctum: self-perception, biased scanning, and signification, gated by choice, latitude of acceptance, publicness, and affirmation, and survive the dysfunctional hall where presenting depression deepens depression and inflated self-presentations breed imposters.
key_concepts: When facing a self-presentational dilemma, people may respond in a principled or authentic fashion, presenting themselves consistently with their private self-images regardless of what the target values, either because others have information that would discredit inauthentic impressions (Schlenker, 1975) or as a matter of principle.

Deceptive self-presentation involves projecting a public image that the person knows is inconsistent with how he or she really is but conforms to the target's values, and such dissimulation ranges from small exaggerations to absolute lies.

Three factors determine the degree to which people stretch their self-presentations beyond the bounds of truthfulness: the person's view of the seriousness of the deception, the likelihood that others will detect the deception, and the perceived incentive of the self-presentational deceit (Baumeister & Jones, 1978; Tesser & Moore, 1986).

One reason people present false images of themselves is insecurity, because people with low self-esteem consider themselves deficient in certain respects and may try to hide their true selves and convey what they view as more acceptable impressions, whereas persons who think more highly of themselves proudly let others see the real them without lying about their personal characteristics or feelings (Elliott, 1982).

The Machiavellianism Scale consists of statements taken directly from Machiavelli's writings as well as others made up by researchers (Christie & Geis, 1970), and people who score high in Machiavellianism tend to live in calculated, strategic manners, holding a utilitarian rather than a moral view of their interactions with others and being more likely to use fabricated self-presentations, such as appearing deferential and ingratiating, when doing so is in their best interests (Blumstein, 1973).

Studies have shown that high Machs are more effective in interpersonal settings, being better at negotiating and bargaining, better able to stand up against social pressure, and better at lying without being detected, since observers in one study could not differentiate truthful from lying high Machs but could tell when low Machs were lying (Geis & Moon, 1981).

When people do not think that accurate self-presentations on a certain dimension will be well-received, they may try to withhold information relevant to that dimension, a tactic involving the attempt to exclude or edit particular self-relevant information from the images one conveys (exclusionary self-presentation) or to behave in ways that evade the necessity of ever broaching the issue (evasive self-presentation).

In the Lamphere and Leary (1988) card experiment, when targets preferred introverts, self-perceived extraverts withheld more cards that would have shown them to be extraverted than when the target preferred extraverts, showing that subjects presented less information about themselves when their self-concepts were inconsistent with the target's values, an exclusionary tactic that allows desired impressions without resorting to lying.

One special type of exclusionary self-presentation involves the personal secret, since people conceal information about behavioral indiscretions, traumatic events, and personal failures that might unfavorably affect how others would perceive them.

When people behave in a particular way, their self-concepts sometimes change in line with their behavior through internalization, which may occur because people infer their personal characteristics from observing their own behavior (self-perception theory; Bem, 1972), scan their self-concepts in a biased fashion for consistent information, or receive affirming feedback from other people (signification).

People are more likely to internalize a self-presentation when they feel they had a high degree of choice in presenting that image (Schlenker, 1986), when the image falls within their latitude of acceptance rather than being highly discrepant from their self-concept (Rhodewalt & Agustsdottir, 1986), when the self-description is public rather than private as shown in Tice's (1992) studies, and when others respond to those presentations in approving or affirming ways (Gergen, 1965; Schlenker, 1986).

Self-presentation can have dysfunctional effects on the self, since people who present themselves in a depressed manner actually become more depressed and recall more depressive episodes from their past (Kelly, McKillop, & Neimeyer, 1991), and people who present unrealistically favorable images of themselves are less likely to believe the favorable feedback they receive from others, which may be partly responsible for why some people feel like imposters (Bednar, Wells, & Peterson, 1989).

assets.topic: Scrub the Worry Engine: The Anxiety Formula, Impression Motivation and Impression Efficacy
assets.visual_frame_description: A boiler-room engine with two gauges labeled MOTIVATION (M) and EFFICACY (1-p) feeding a needle on a scale marked SOCIAL ANXIETY, with dials lit for NO MOTIVATION -> NO ANXIETY and FULL CERTAINTY -> NO ANXIETY, and a red warning lamp for M SKY-HIGH / p = 0; alongside, a handshake scene between a stranger and a boss, a blank script page marked NO SCRIPT -> DOUBT, and a noisy construction site where a speaker's pulse needle drops once a sign reads NOISE EXPLAINS EVERYTHING, with a caption reading Worry = Wanting It x Doubting You Can Get It.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to scrub through the machinery of social anxiety: start with the fact that the most common causes of anxiety are social situations, then take apart the formula SA = M x (1 - p), where impression motivation times doubt in self-presentational efficacy produces anxiety. Walk the boundaries: no motivation means no anxiety, total certainty means no anxiety, and the worst case is sky-high motivation with zero chance of success. Then clear away the misinterpretations: people sometimes want negative impressions, and people can feel anxious even when they know they are making good impressions but not good enough. Finally, audit the situational antecedents: first encounters with strangers, powerful people on whom we depend, uncertain scripts and novel roles, and how a distracting noise that explains away poor performance actually lowers anxious arousal, from the Leary (1986) experiment to the curious popularity of singles bars.
key_concepts: According to the self-presentational theory (Leary, 1983c; Schlenker & Leary, 1982b), people experience social anxiety when they are motivated to make desired impressions on other people but doubt that they will be able to successfully make those impressions.
Social anxiety is a function of two things, impression motivation (M) and the perceived probability of self-presentational success (p), as expressed in the formula SA = M x (1 - p) (Leary, 1983c).

If a person does not care how he or she is regarded in a particular situation, that is, if impression motivation is zero, the person will not experience any social anxiety regardless of the value of p.

No matter how motivated people are to make an impression, they do not feel anxious if they are certain that others will form the desired impression of them, because when the subjective probability of making the desired impression is 1.00 the person should not feel socially anxious.

The worst possible situation from a self-presentational standpoint is one in which the person is exceptionally motivated to make a desired impression but something has happened to make the person believe he or she has no chance of making that impression, as when an interview for your dream job goes badly.

Some researchers have misinterpreted the theory as suggesting that social anxiety arises when people think they will make negative or unfavorable impressions, but this is incorrect because people sometimes want to make negative, socially undesirable impressions, such as appearing intimidating, helpless, or incompetent.

People may feel socially anxious even when they know they are making good impressions if they do not think they are being perceived favorably enough to accomplish their goals, as when a job applicant, political candidate, or adolescent on a first date needs a stronger impression than the one being made.

Because people know that first impressions are particularly important, they are more motivated to make desired impressions the first few times they meet a particular person, and as a result people feel especially anxious when they meet new people or interact with strangers (Leary, 1983c).

People are more motivated to be perceived in particular ways by those who have power over their lives, so they feel more socially anxious when dealing with their employers or other powerful people than with people on whom they are not dependent.

In the initial study that tested the self-presentation model (Leary, 1980), subjects who were told how to make a desired impression on another person reported feeling less anxious than subjects who were not told how to make a desired impression.

Without a script about how to behave, people are likely to have doubts about their impression efficacy, which explains why encounters involving strangers, ambiguity, or novel roles often evoke considerable anxiety, and people will feel more comfortable about new situations the more they can find out about what is likely to happen.

In Leary's (1986) experiment, subjects who were told that distracting noise would interfere with the other person's ability to form accurate impressions of them had lower pulse rates than subjects told the noise would have little effect, and the popularity of singles bars may reflect that, with everything working against effective impression management, no one needs to be too concerned about rejection.

assets.topic: Dialogue on the Trait Ledger: Trait Social Anxiety, Social Phobia, and Appearance and Physique Anxiety
assets.visual_frame_description: A two-sided courtroom stage: on the anxious side, a figure stares at a stack of questionnaires (I often feel nervous even in casual get-togethers) while a monitor shows a glance from a stranger inflating into a verdict of WORSE IMPRESSION THAN EVERYONE THINKS; on the body side, a mirror reflects a scale marked BODY FAT, a scrawny man flexing, and a queue of 100,000 silhouettes filing toward a surgical theater, while a caption reads Every Child Learns: The Body Is The Pecking Order.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to stage a dialogue on why some people are anxious a great deal of the time: define trait social anxiety and the self-report measures that ask how often and intensely people feel nervous in social situations, then cross-examine the psychiatric classification of social phobia as a persistent fear of being humiliated or embarrassed under scrutiny. Interrogate the evidence: socially anxious people score higher in public self-consciousness, think more about the impressions they are making, assume they made worse impressions even from a mere glance, and carry lower self-esteem because they assume others see them as they see themselves. Then bring the body into the dock: children learn that bodily features determine the pecking order, our culture's obsession with body fat, men's worry about looking scrawny, women's worry about weight and breast size, the 100,000 cosmetic surgeries a year, and why female college students score higher on appearance and physique anxiety than males.
key_concepts: People who are particularly likely to feel anxious in social encounters are said to be high in trait social anxiety, which is also called dispositional social anxiety or social anxiousness.

Psychologists have developed several self-report scales to measure trait social anxiety, and although differences exist among them, all of these measures ask subjects how often or intensely they feel nervous in social situations.

People who are so high in trait social anxiety that their lives are severely affected are called socially phobic, a psychiatric classification for people with a persistent fear of one or more social situations in which they are exposed to possible scrutiny by others and fear that they may do something humiliating or embarrassing (American Psychiatric Association, 1987).

The self-presentational approach suggests that some people are higher in trait social anxiety than others because they are more motivated to make impressions on other people and/or are less likely to think they will do so, and according to this view social phobics are extraordinarily concerned about others' impressions of them.

In support of this model, socially anxious people score higher in public self-consciousness, are more aware of others' impressions of them, and tend to be more concerned about being perceived unfavorably and being evaluated negatively (Buss, 1980; Hope & Heimberg, 1988), and they also report thinking more about the impressions they're making on others in laboratory conversations than subjects low in social anxiety (Leary, 1986).

Socially anxious and shy people consistently think that they are making less favorable impressions on other people than subjects low in social anxiety, and in one study socially anxious subjects assumed they had made a worse impression even if the other person had only glanced at them (Leary, Kowalski, & Campbell, 1988).

Socially anxious people tend to have lower self-esteem than less anxious people, and because people tend to assume that others see them pretty much as they see themselves, low self-esteem per se does not lead to social anxiety but is mediated by the person's assumptions about how he or she is regarded by others.

As VanderVelde (1985) pointed out, every child learns that such bodily features as size, weight, strength, complexion, or looks are used with often painful accuracy by peers, classmates, teachers, and coaches to determine the pecking order in social and athletic activities, and bodily flaws become social liabilities and ever-present potentials for rejection and humiliation.

Of primary concern in our culture is the amount of body fat one has, and many people become absolutely distraught when they think they've gained (or failed to lose) weight, though as Leary notes we are not really worried about how much we weigh but about how fat we look.

Other aspects of physique that people find distressing include musculature, with men in particular worrying about looking too scrawny, while women tend to worry about being overweight and about the size of their breasts, and each year approximately 100,000 American women undergo cosmetic surgery to change the size of their breasts (Findlay, 1988).

People who are physique anxious feel particularly nervous or uncomfortable when others seem to be evaluating their bodies, report thinking more negative thoughts about their bodies, and tend to be more worried about others' evaluations generally and more likely to be high in trait social anxiety (Hart, Leary, & Rejeski, 1989).

In American culture, weight and appearance are considered more important aspects of a woman's social image than a man's, so female college students tend to score higher on measures of appearance and physique anxiety than male students, and in one study 70 percent of the female respondents surveyed thought they were overweight and wanted to lose an average of 14 pounds each (Miller, Linke, & Linke, 1980).

assets.topic: Audit the Behavioral Ledger: Avoidance, Withdrawal and Inhibition, Innocuous Sociability, and Protective Self-Presentation
assets.visual_frame_description: An audit ledger with four columns: under AVOIDANCE, a figure ducks out of a conference-room door marked THREAT; under WITHDRAWAL, a silent employee shrinks in a chair at the boss's party while a tally board shows a group losing its quiet member's ideas and everyone else growing quieter too; under INNOCUOUS SOCIABILITY, a nervous guest nods, smiles, and murmurs uh-huh while a spotlight stays pointed at the talkative host; under PROTECTIVE, a respondent shades every answer toward the middle of the scale, stamped TYPICAL = SAFE, until a stamp reading PARADOX lands over a frown: Less Liking, More Discomfort.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to audit what socially anxious people actually do: start with the extreme of avoiding threatening situations altogether, which both reduces anxiety and preempts undesired impressions, then trace social withdrawal, noting that anxious people only withdraw from others when the anxiety is self-presentational, since people afraid of physical pain actually prefer company. Log the group costs: quiet members deprive groups of their ideas and their silence suppresses others' participation. Then audit the counter-tactic of innocuous sociability: nodding, verbally agreeing, back-channeling, smiling, and looking at others more, which keeps the focus off oneself and conveys quiet friendliness. Close the books on protective self-presentation (Arkin, 1981): conveying as little as possible, presenting oneself as typical and average, behaving cautiously, and the paradox that these safe tactics can backfire into less liking and greater discomfort in interaction partners.
key_concepts: In the extreme case, people may avoid altogether situations in which they doubt they will make desired impressions, and avoiding such situations serves two functions: it reduces their level of anxiety, and it preempts the possibility of making undesired impressions.

People who become uncomfortable in a social encounter may socially withdraw while remaining physically present, as when an employee who feels out of place at the boss's party is unusually quiet and reserved, and research shows that people who score high on measures of trait social anxiety generally talk less in conversations (Leary, 1983c).

Contrary to what you might think, social withdrawal is not a typical response to anxiety, because when people are anxious or afraid for nonsocial reasons, such as when they're afraid of experiencing physical pain, they actually prefer to interact with other people (Schachter, 1959), and they only withdraw from others when they are anxious for self-presentational reasons.

From the standpoint of self-presentation theory, withdrawal is a reasonable response to self-presentational worries, because if you don't think you'll make the impression you desire, continuing to interact carries quite a risk, and pulling back and being quiet is socially adaptive rather than helpless resignation.

The quality of a group's decisions depends in large part on the active participation of all group members, so if some group members are afraid to contribute their ideas out of fear of being perceived negatively, the group cannot benefit from their ideas and expertise, and their quietness seems to reduce the participation of other group members (Camacho & Paulhus, 1993).

People who feel socially anxious often adopt an interpersonal style called innocuous sociability, by which people who are worried about the impressions they are making can remain engaged in an interaction in a manner that presents little additional risk to their social identities.

Socially anxious individuals tend to agree more with other people, both by nodding their heads (Pilkonis, 1977) and by verbally agreeing (Leary, Knight, & Johnson, 1987), use more back-channel responses, the sounds that indicate active listening such as uh-huh, oh, and hmmmm (Natale, Entin, & Jaffe, 1979), and also seem to smile more and look at others more even though they feel uncomfortable (Cheek & Buss, 1981; Pilkonis, 1977).

Innocuous sociability helps to keep the focus of the conversation on other people and off oneself, because nodding, back-channeling, and smiling encourage others to dominate the conversation, and it conveys an impression of quiet friendliness and interest that can actually create a mildly positive impression.

When people do not think they will make the impressions they want to make, they often adopt a protective self-presentation style (Arkin, 1981), so rather than attempting to make a good impression through acquisitive self-presentation, the socially anxious person tries to avoid making a bad impression (Shepperd & Arkin, 1990).

One protective self-presentation strategy is simply to convey as little information about oneself as possible, since talking less will usually not make a good impression on other people but it also will not make a bad impression.

Socially anxious people present themselves as more typical, that is, as closer to the average of all subjects' ratings, than subjects low in social anxiety, a safe tactic because coming across as pretty much like everybody else is not likely to make a particularly good impression but is not likely to make a bad one either, and another study showed socially anxious people generally present themselves more cautiously than lows (Leary, 1986).

Paradoxically, this seemingly safe, protective style of self-presentation can sometimes backfire, since on occasion the self-protective behaviors of socially anxious people are associated with less liking and greater discomfort in the people who interact with them (Meleshko & Alden, 1993), so their self-presentational worries may lead them to behave in ways that cause others to form less positive impressions.

assets.topic: Matrix Match: Attention and Memory, Choking under Pressure, and the Self-Handicapping Grid
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall matrix with columns: IMPRESSION FOCUS, MEMORY, CHOKING, and SELF-HANDICAP. Under IMPRESSION FOCUS, a mind split between What is he/she thinking? and a speech balloon marked Boy, that was stupid; under MEMORY, a handshake dissolves a name card labeled NEVER ENCODED while a graph shows words before your turn vanishing (26% remembered after, 11% before); under CHOKING, a football kicker freezes mid-swing as a coach's time-out sign ticks over his thoughts, and a trembling pianist's fingers knot; under SELF-HANDICAP, a row of pill bottles labeled ACTAVIL (enhances) and PANDOCRIN (disrupts) stands in public light where three of four hands reach for the disrupting one, while a private booth shows none, with a caption reading Protect The Image, Even At The Cost Of The Performance.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to build a matrix of cognitive breakdown under self-presentational pressure: drop cards for impression focus, the state in which monitoring how one comes across dominates thought and drains the cognitive resources needed for other tasks, and trace the memory failures it causes, from forgetting a newly introduced name (which was never encoded) to Kimble and Zehr's finding that visible subjects remembered less, Baumeister's finding that conscious impression-making lowers recall, test anxiety's self-preoccupation, and the next-in-line effect in which high social anxiety subjects remembered 26 percent of words after their turn but only 11 percent before it. Then run the choking column: inferior performance under pressure from two causes, conscious attention to automatic behaviors (the athlete who thinks about the kick and chokes) and physical tension. Finally, lay out the behavioral self-handicapping grid: Berglas and Jones' definition, the sabotaging drug choices of threatened subjects, and the Kolditz and Arkin experiment in which three-fourths of public subjects chose the performance-debilitating drug while no private subjects did.
key_concepts: People who are concerned about the impressions they are making are likely to be in a state of impression focus where impression monitoring dominates their thoughts as they wonder how others are perceiving them, and devoting excessive attention to one's impressions can divert a person's cognitive resources from other tasks.

When people are excessively preoccupied with their self-presentations, they pay less attention to what is going on around them, so people who are thinking about their social images are less likely to remember information they hear than people who are not impression-focused, and when we fail to recall a person's name moments after being introduced, most likely we were thinking about other things, including how best to respond, and didn't encode the person's name into memory, so although we might say we forgot the name, the truth is that we never really learned it to begin with.

In Kimble and Zehr's (1982) study, subjects who could be seen by the other person in an interaction remembered less information than those who could not be seen, presumably because they were more preoccupied with the other person's impressions.

A study by Baumeister, Hutton, and Tice (1989) suggested that the more people think consciously about making a particular impression, the less they remember about a social interaction, and subjects high in social anxiety had difficulty remembering what happened while they were being scrutinized by other people (Lord, Saenz, & Godfrey, 1987).

When people experience test anxiety, they find it difficult to recall things they have learned because they are thinking about how poorly they are doing and the disastrous consequences of failing, and this anxious self-preoccupation interferes with their ability to think about the test questions themselves (Wine, 1971), so many, if not most, instances of test anxiety are self-presentational.

The next-in-line effect is the finding that when people are waiting to perform in a social situation, they have difficulty remembering information that is presented just before they are to perform (Bond & Omar, 1990; Brenner, 1973), because they are too busy thinking about how they are going to present themselves to listen to what the other person is saying.

In Bond and Omar's (1990) study, subjects high in social anxiety remembered 26 percent of the words that followed them but only 11 percent of those that immediately preceded them, whereas subjects low in social anxiety remembered virtually the same number of words both before and after they spoke, and social anxiety was inversely related to memory for preceding words.

Choking under pressure refers to inferior performance that occurs despite individual striving and situational demands for superior performance (Baumeister, 1984), and people choke when the pressures of performing lead them to perform far below the level of which they are capable.

One process underlying choking is that when people become worried about how they are being perceived by others, they sometimes begin to pay conscious attention to behaviors that are normally mindless, habitual, and automatic, and experienced athletes who begin to think about otherwise habitual movements may choke (Baumeister & Steinhilber, 1984).

The second cause of choking is physical tension, since many actions are difficult to perform when one is physically tense or, worse, trembling from anxiety, and concerns with others' impressions often lead to social anxiety, which is accompanied by bodily tension.

Berglas and Jones (1978) defined self-handicapping as any action or choice of performance setting that enhances the opportunity to externalize (or excuse) failure and to internalize (reasonably accept credit for) success, so the presence of the self-created impediment insulates the individual to some degree from the implications of failure.

In Kolditz and Arkin's (1982) experiment, subjects were most likely to choose Pandocrin, the drug they thought would interfere with their performance, when they had worked unsolvable problems, thought the researcher would score their tests, and made their drug choice in public, with three-fourths of subjects whose scores and drug choices were public choosing the debilitating drug while no subjects whose scores and drug choices were private chose it, and people who score high in public self-consciousness self-handicap more than those who score low (Shepperd & Arkin, 1989).

assets.topic: Boss Level: Self-Reported Handicaps, Other-Enhancement, and the Health Hazard Gauntlet
assets.visual_frame_description: A boss arena shaped like a hazard gauntlet: at the gate, a claim form reads ANXIETY AND TRAUMA ACCEPTED AS EXCUSES (self-reported handicaps); mid-way, a tennis player hands her expensive racket to her opponent while a professor slides office keys to a younger colleague, both stamped UNWAVERINGLY UNSELFISH; at the far end, a condom box blushes at a drugstore counter (30% EMBARRASSED), a bedroom freezes on a hand holding a condom marked TOO BOLD, a gay man shrugs WIMP? over one-third of encounters, and an exam room shows a woman under a gown marked BETTER COVERAGE = MORE COMFORT while a psychiatric office door labeled STIGMA keeps a patient outside, with a caption reading Worrying About Impressions Can Be Hazardous To Your Health.
assets.player_mission: Your mission is to defeat the final boss, the full arc of self-presentational worries: first claim the verbal handicaps, the self-reported handicaps (Leary & Shepperd, 1986) that let people claim anxiety and traumatic pasts as excuses when those claims are plausible explanations for poor performance. Then deploy other-enhancement (Shepperd & Arkin, 1991): boosting a competitor's performance so poor results are attributed to the opponent's advantage, while scoring points for being unselfish and cooperative, and see it paired with self-handicapping in the tennis player lending her racket and the professor giving up research space. Finally, clear the health hazard gauntlet: condom avoidance driven by embarrassment about buying them and introducing them, the fear of appearing to have anticipated sex or to distrust a partner, the gay men who risked unprotected anal intercourse rather than look like wimps, and the medical attention gauntlet where embarrassment over gynecological, rectal, and breast exams deters testing, better gowns ease anxiety, and the stigma of mental health care keeps people out of treatment centers.
key_concepts: Even when people do not behaviorally self-handicap, they can usually claim that they are operating under a handicap, and these verbal claims are called self-reported handicaps (Leary & Shepperd, 1986).

People report experiencing more anxiety while taking a test when they are told that anxiety is a viable explanation for poor performance on the test (Smith, Snyder, & Handelsman, 1982), and socially anxious men report feeling more anxious when they believe that anxiety can account for a poor social performance (Snyder & Smith, 1986).

People also report that they are handicapped by traumatic events in their past, advertising past adversities so others will know they are operating with an ongoing handicap, and in a laboratory demonstration subjects reported having experienced more traumatic events in their lives when they thought that a traumatic personal history served as a plausible reason for performing poorly on a test (DeGree & Snyder, 1985).

Behavioral other-enhancement involves enhancing the performance of a competitor (Shepperd & Arkin, 1991), so that by providing opponents or competitors with tools, resources, or other advantages that promote better performance, people hope that their own relatively poor performance will be attributed to the opponent's advantage.

Other-enhancement has a second self-presentational benefit, because in addition to providing a reason why the person did not perform as well as the opponent he or she helped, the person who uses other-enhancement scores points for being unselfish and cooperative.

Often, self-handicapping and other-enhancement occur together, as when a tennis player offers her opponent use of her more expensive racket, which may both advantage her opponent and disadvantage herself, and as when a college professor gives up research space to younger, untenured faculty, now having a good reason why the younger professor is doing more or better research.

Research suggests that the failure to use condoms is not usually due to lack of information about pregnancy, STDs, or condoms, but one primary reason many people do not use condoms is self-presentational: people are often embarrassed about acquiring and/or using condoms (Leary, Tchividjian, & Kraxberger, 1994).

One primary impediment to using condoms is concern about what others will think when one gets them at a drugstore or health center, with 30 percent of respondents in one study reporting being embarrassed when buying condoms (Hanna, 1989), and embarrassment over obtaining condoms was greater than that for acquiring contraceptive pills or foam, which do not protect against AIDS (Herold, 1981).

Even if a person acquires condoms, self-presentational concerns can deter people from actually introducing them into a sexual encounter, since some people worry that having a condom will imply they had anticipated having sex or had actively worked to seduce the other person, and women may be particularly afraid to produce a condom because they will appear sexually experienced or too bold.

Some people think that suggesting that they and their partners use a condom may convey a lack of trust (Catania et al., 1991), and in one study of gay men's reasons for having anal intercourse without a condom, one reason was a fear of making a negative impression, with over one-third of respondents indicating that such concerns had led them to have unprotected anal intercourse (Gold, Skinner, Grant, & Plummer, 1991).

Some medical examinations create self-presentational anxieties because they involve parts of the body that people consider private, and studies of cervical screening exams and mammography showed that embarrassment regarding these procedures deterred some women from being tested, and although attempts to reduce women's anxiety by having physicians explain the procedures as they occur have not generally reduced anxiety or discomfort, Williams, Park, and Kline (1992) showed that simply using a gown that more adequately covers the patient's body increases patient comfort.

People's willingness to seek medical care is also affected by worries about the impressions that people will form if the fact they sought medical care becomes known, so much has been written about the stigma of seeing a psychiatrist, psychologist, or other mental health professional, and people are often reluctant to enter treatment centers for alcohol and drug abuse because of their concerns about what people in the treatment setting and in the outside world will think of them.
